passages.text: Vipers (family Viperidae) are a monophyletic lineage of venomous snakes found across Eurasia, Africa, and America, and have received extensive research attention primarily due to their medical relevance. The majority of venom studies in this group have primarily been investigated using a proteomic approach, with early venom work being highly motivated by the medical field, with a limited number of studies employing genomic approaches (but see. Sequencing efforts to obtain high-quality reference genomes have mainly focused on pitvipers (Crotalinae subfamily, 11 reference genomes, NCBI last accessed 13 March 2024), especially within the Crotalus (n = 6) genus, and have focused on the study of venom evolution. Other viperids have also been sequenced (although in lower numbers) from both Azemiopinae and Viperinae subfamilies (one and four, respectively). Currently, reference genomes are only available for 16 viper species out of the total 387 total species via the NCBI genomic database. Vipers display extensive variation in venom composition between and within genera and even intraspecifically. Such differences are most likely due to the high diversity of venom genes and their different effects on prey, but are also, at least in some cases, the result of introgression with related species. This provides an extraordinary opportunity to study trait evolution both at inter- and intraspecific levels.

Native to the Arabian Peninsula, the Arabian horned viper (Cerastes gasperettii, family Viperidae) is a venomous snake currently recognized within the highest medical importance category (WHO; accessed July, 2024). Extending from the Sinai Peninsula to southwestern Iran in the north and reaching as far as Yemen and Oman in the south, its distribution is widespread (Supplementary Fig. S1). Found mainly in sandy habitats, this arid-adapted ground-dwelling snake with generalist requirements is one of the most common venomous snakes found in Arabia and is responsible for occasional snakebite envenomations.

In this study, we present a high-quality chromosome-level reference genome assembly for C. gasperettii (NCBI: txid110202), being one of the first within the Viperinae subfamily. Our highly contiguous genome showcases a high level of similarity at the chromosome level within the Viperidae family with some minor rearrangements with elapids. Moreover, combining genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, we characterized the main toxins found in its venom and the location of those toxins in the genome, comparing their evolutionary history and gene copy number variation with those of other venomous species. We deciphered its adequate levels of genetic diversity. Finally, we reconstructed the demographic history for the species, revealing how historical increases in aridity likely drove population expansions. Overall, the genomic resources generated in this study provide an essential reference resource for forthcoming studies on venom evolution.
Methods
Sampling

Three adult specimens (two females and one male) of C. gasperettii gasperettii were used for this study (Supplementary Table S1). Blood was extracted only from a single female individual (the heterogametic sex, sample CG1) to obtain high-molecular-weight (HMW) genomic DNA (gDNA). We anesthesized the individual, extracted blood from the heart, and stored this in ethanol and EDTA. For each of the 3 individuals, we extracted 12 different tissues, including the venom gland, which was stored in RNAlater until RNA extraction (Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Fig. S2). Before dissections, venom was extracted and snakes were allowed to recover for 4 days to maximize the venom gland transcription. We only extracted the left venom gland per individual because previous research within the same family has shown that both venom glands provide indistinguishable results.
DNA extraction, library preparation and sequencing

We extracted gDNA from the blood of a female individual (CG1 in Supplementary Table S1) using the MagAttract HMW Kit (Qiagen, Germany) following the manufacturer's protocols without modifications. Then, we sequenced a total of two 8 M SMRT HiFi cells in a Sequel II PacBio machine, aiming for a ~30x of coverage, at the University of Leiden. Hi-C libraries were prepared using the Omni-C kit (Dovetail Genomics), following the manufacturer's protocol and using blood stored in EDTA, at the National Center for Genomic Analyses (CNAG), in Barcelona, Spain. The library was paired-end sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 (2 x 150 bp) following the manufacturer's protocol for dual indexing and aiming for a coverage of ~60x. Finally, we sequenced short-read whole-genome data of the same individual using a NEB Ultra II FS DNA kit; the library was paired-end sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 (2 x 150 bp) at the Core sequencing platform from the New York University of Abu Dhabi, aiming for ~70x depth of coverage.
RNA extraction, library preparationm and sequencing

We extracted RNA from the same 3 individuals described above (Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Fig. S2). RNA was isolated using a HighPurity Total RNA Extraction Kit (Canvax, Valladolid, Spain). We selected a total of 35 samples (Supplementary Table S2). RNA libraries were prepared with the VAHTS Universal V8 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit, and being strand-specific, were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 (2 x 150 bp) aiming for an average of 40 M read pairs per sample (Supplementary Table S2), but we first sequenced the reference individual and subsequently the other 2 samples. Moreover, we sequenced one 8 M SMRT HiFi cell on a Sequel II PacBio machine containing 2 Iso-seq HiFi libraries at the University of Leiden: one containing only the venom gland, and the second library being a pool of 8 high-quality tissues (brain, kidney, liver, gallbladder, spleen, tongue, pancreas, and ovary).
Genome assembly and scaffolding

Quality control of HiFi and Illumina reads was performed using FastQC (RRID:SCR_014583) v.0.12.1 and adapters were removed with cutadapt (RRID:SCR_011814) v.4.9. In order to initially explore the genome size, heterozygosity levels, and coverage data, we generated a k-mer profile with Meryl (RRID:SCR_026366) v.1.4.1, using the raw HiFi reads and default parameters, and visualized it with GenomeScope2 (RRID:SCR_017014) v.2.0.1. Then, we assembled the genome following the VGP assembly pipeline v.2.0. PacBio HiFi reads were assembled into contigs using the software Hifiasm (RRID:SCR_021069) v.0.21.0, producing primary and alternate assemblies. We used purge_dups (RRID:SCR_021173) to remove haplotypic duplicates from the primary assembly and added them to the alternate assembly. Then, we scaffolded the resulting haplotypic assembly using the Hi-C data with SALSA2 (Salsa, RRID:SCR_022013) v.1, with default parameters. Following the VGP assembly pipeline, manual curation was performed with Pretext (RRID:SCR_022024) v.0.2.5. Breaks were not manually created and we joint contings on gaps previously identified by SALSA2 (Salsa, RRID:SCR_022013). We used the ~78x Illumina data to polish the assembly with one round of Pilon (RRID:SCR_014731) v.1.24. The mitochondrial genome was obtained with GetOrganelle (RRID:SCR_022963) v.1.7.7.1, using the available mitochondrial genome of several Echis species (E. coloratus, E. carinatus, and E. omanensis) to seed the assembly (NCBI: SRX18902082, SRX18902083, SRX18902084, respectively).
Genome assembly quality evaluation

Quality assessment and general metrics for the final assembly were estimated with both QUAST (Quast, RRID:SCR_011228) v.5.1.0 and gfastats (RRID:SCR_026368) v.1.3.8. Possible contaminations were evaluated with BlobToolKit (Blobtools, RRID:SCR_017618) v.4.4.0 using the NCBI taxdump database. We also used MitoFinder v.1.4.2 to confirm that the mitochondrial genome was absent in the assembled nuclear reference genome. Completeness of the genome assembly was assessed with BUSCO (Busco, RRID:SCR_015008) v.5.3.0. against the sauropsida_odb10 database (n = 7,480).
Genome annotation

First, we identified repetitive elements using RepeatModeler (RRID:SCR_015027) v.2.0.3 for de novo predictions of repeat families. To annotate genome-wide complex repeats, we used RepeatMasker (RRID:SCR_012954) v.4.1.3 with default settings to identify known Tetrapoda repeats present in the curated Repbase database. Then, we ran 3 iterative rounds of RepeatMasker to annotate the known and unknown elements identified by RepeatModeler in order to maximize the known elements at the expense of diminishing the unknown elements. Later, we soft-masked the genome for simple repeats. We used GeMoMa (GeMoMa, RRID:SCR_017646) v.1.9 to annotate protein-coding genes, combining both the RNA-seq data generated in this study as described above (already mapped in to our new assembly) as well as annotations from 6 other squamate genomes already published: Crotalus adamanteus, Crotalus tigris, Ophiophagus hannah, Naja naja, Crotalus ruber and Crotalus viridis. We quality checked and removed the adapters of the RNA-seq data using fastp v.0.23.3, as well as mapped the transcriptomic data to our new reference genome with Hisat2 (RRID:SCR_015530) v.2.2.1. Additionally, we also removed the adapters for the Iso-seq data with fastp (RRID:016962) v.0.23.3 and mapped the long-read transcriptomic data to our new reference genome with pbmm2 (RRID:SCR_025549), collapsing mapped reads into unique isoforms with isoseq3 and annotating with GeneMarkS-T (GeneMark, RRID:SCR_011930) v.5.1. We combined both annotations (GeMoMa and GeneMarkS-T) with TSEBRA. We BLASTp (blastp, RRID:SCR_001010) our predicted proteins to a Uniprot protein database for a total of 10 species (C. gasperettii, C. vipera, C. cerastes, Anolis carolinensis, C. viridis, C. tigris, C. ruber, C. adamanteus, O. hannah and N. naja). Simultaneously, we ran Interproscan v.5.72 on our predicted proteins. Then, we combined both functional annotations with AGAT v.1.4.1. Finally, as toxin-coding gene families are known to occur in large tandem arrays and the number of paralogs can be underestimated in particular gene families, we performed additional annotation steps for toxin genes: Following, we used a combination of empirical annotation in FGENESH+ (FGENESH, RRID:SCR_011928), as well as manual annotation using RNA-seq and Iso-seq alignments; the former identified all genes regardless of expression, whereas the latter was used to explicitly identify expressed toxins.
Chromosome-level analyses

Chromosomal synteny was explored between our new chromosome-level reference genome for the Arabian horned viper together with the Eastern diamondback rattlesnake (C. adamanteus), the Indian cobra (N. naja), and the brown anole (Anolis sagrei) using MCscan (RRID:SCR_017650) v.1.4.23. Protein sequences from each of the 3 venomous snakes were extracted using AGAT v.1.2.1 and were pairwise aligned with LAST, implemented in the JCVI python module. A first alignment was used between the 3 species to identify chromosomes assembled in the reverse complement, which were corrected using SAMtools faidx (samtools, RRID:SCR_002105) v.1.18.1 using both options reverse-complement and mark-strand. Gene annotations for the new reference (with the corresponding reversed chromosomes) were annotated using GeMoMa v.1.9, and MCscan was rerun. The last 4 scaffolds (14, 15, 16, and 17) from A. sagrei were removed because no orthologous groups were found.
Transcriptomics

After adapter trimming and quality control using fastp v.0.23.3, we mapped our RNA-seq reads to the reference genome of C. gasperettii using Hisat2 (RRID:SCR_015530) v.2.2.1. Gene expression raw counts per gene across all samples were calculated with StringTie (RRID:SCR_016323). Initial exploration of our transcriptomic data revealed a clear batch effect for one of the 3 samples (Supplementary Fig. S4), due to the low mapping of that sample to our reference genome. Therefore, we decided to remove individual CG1 from future RNA-seq analyses. Moreover, to avoid pseudoreplication, we also removed the accessory gland from individual CG009 due to its high similarity with the venom gland, suggesting that the venom gland rather than the accessory gland was sampled (Supplementary  Fig. S4). Differential expression analyses were carried out with the DESeq2 package (RRID:SCR_015687) v.1.42.0 from R v.4.4.2. Prior to analysis, genes with <10 counts across all samples were filtered out. For comparisons, we defined 2 groups: venom glands versus all other tissues. DESeq2 uses a negative binomial generalized linear model to estimate differences in gene expression, and the P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate. Genes with an adjusted P-value <0.01 and a fold change (FC) >2 were considered significantly differentially expressed. Finally, we identified the highly expressed genes found in the venom gland as well as the toxins uniquely expressed in the venom gland (following) which were defined as: (1) genes expressed in the venom gland (transcripts per million (TPM) > 500), (2) differential upregulated genes with a FC > 2 comparing venom glands with all other tissues, and (3) unique to venom glands (TPM < 500 in all other tissues).
Proteomics

A bottom-up mass spectrometry (MS) strategy was used to characterize the venom of C. gasperettii. Briefly, the venom proteome (pooled from individuals CN6134 and CN6135, both from the United Arab Emirates (UAE); Supplementary Table S1) was submitted to reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography decomplexation followed by SDS-PAGE analysis in 12% polyacrylamide gels run under non-reducing and reducing conditions. Protein bands were excised from Coomassie Brilliant Blue-stained gels and subjected to automated in-gel reduction and alkylation on a Genomics Solution ProGest Protein Digestion Workstation. Tryptic digests were submitted to MS/MS analysis on a nano-Acquity UltraPerformance LC (UPLC) equipped with a BEH130 C18 (100 microm x 100 mm, 1.7 microm particle size) column in-line with a Waters SYNAPT G2 high-definition mass spectrometer. Doubly and triply charged ions were selected for CID-MS/MS. Fragmentation spectra were matched against a customized database including the bony vertebrates taxonomy dataset of the NCBI nonredundant database (release 258, 15 October 2023) plus the species-specific venom gland transcriptomic and genomic protein sequences gathered in this work. Search parameters were as follows: enzyme: trypsin (two-missed cleavage allowed); MS/MS mass tolerance for monoisotopic ions: +-0.6 Da; carbamidomethyl cysteine and oxidation of methionine were selected as fixed and variable modifications, respectively. Assignments with significance protein score threshold of P < 0.05 (Mascot score > 43) were taken into consideration, and all associated peptide ion hits were manually validated. Unmatched MS/MS spectra were de novo sequenced and manually matched to homologous snake toxins available in the NCBI nonredundant protein sequences database using the default parameters of the BLASTP program.
Local synteny analyses

To explore toxin genomic organization across (sub)families, we used BLASTn, incorporating both toxin and nontoxin paralogs to identify the genomic location of SVMPs, SVSPs, and PLA2 toxin families, across the genome of C. gasperettii, C. adamanteus, N. naja and A. feae. We excluded A. feae for SVSP and SVMP local synteny analyses because those families were not assembled onto a single contig in the A. feae genome. Then, we aligned those regions using Mafft: for SVMPs in CHR8:16.506.135 to CHR8:17.374.029, for SVSPs in CHR9: 17.531.416 to CHR9:17.788.049 and for PLA2 in CHR17:7.882.542 to CHR17:7.916.827 Each species was annotated within the MSA using its own annotation as a reference in Geneious Prime 2023.0.4. Results were plotted using the gggenomes package from R v.4.4.2.
Toxin phylogenies

We used phylogenetic inference to study the evolutionary history for the main groups of toxins (i.e., SVMPs and SVSPs), which were the most abundant in the proteome of C. gasperettii, as well as PLA2 because this family has been widely studied within the Viperidae family. For the 3 main toxin families, we selected available toxin genes as well as nontoxin paralogous genes from venomous species; we also included other nontoxin paralogous genes from nontoxic species (for details, see Supplementary Datasets for the 3 main toxins). When nuclear sequences were obtained, we translated CDS to protein sequence, and then protein sequences were aligned with Mafft (RRID:SCR_011811) v.7. Following, we built a phylogeny for each of the toxin groups with the translated CDS sequences, as explained above, using Phyml (RRID:SCR_014629) v.3.3, implementing the Dayhoff substitution model and validating our inferred tree with aBayes support.
Demographic history

We inferred the demographic history of C. gasperettii by implementing the Pairwise Sequential Markovian Coalescent (PSMC) software (RRID:SCR_017229) v.0.6.5 on the short-read whole-genome data. Heterozygous positions were obtained from bam files with the Samtools v.1.9 mpileup function, and data were filtered for low mapping (<30) and base quality (<30). Minimum and maximum depths were set at a third (27x) and twice (156x) the average coverage. Only autosomal chromosomes were considered. We used a squamate mutation rate of 2.4 x 10-9 substitutions/site/generation and a generation time of 3 years, following, respectively. A total of 10 bootstraps were calculated, plotting the final results with the psmc_plot.pl function from PSMC.
Genomic diversity

We downloaded Illumina data for Bothrops jararaca (SRR13839751 from, Crotalus viridis (SRR19221440), Naja kaouthia (SRR8224383), N. naja (SRR10428156) and Sistrurus tergeminus (SRR12802282). Then, we filtered for quality (Phred score: 30) and removed adapters with fastp v.0.23.3. Trimming of poly-G/X tails and correction in overlapped regions were specified. All other parameters were set as default. Filtered sequences were visually explored with FastQC (fastQC, RRID:SCR_014583) v.0.12.1 to ensure data quality and absence of adapters. C. gasperettii filtered reads were mapped against the new reference genome of C. gasperettii using the bwa mem algorithm (bwa, RRID:SCR_010910) v.0.7.17. B. jararaca, C. viridis, and S. tergeminus were mapped against the C. viridis reference genome and N. naja and N. kaouthia were mapped against the N. naja reference genome. Mapped reads were sorted with Samtools (RRID:SCR_002105) v,1.9 and duplicated reads were marked and removed with PicardTools (Picard, RRID:SCR_006525) v,2.28.0. Reads with mapping quality <30 were discarded. SNP calling was carried out with HaplotypeCaller (GATK, RRID:SCR_001876) v.4.1.3.0, with BP_resolution and split by chromosome. For each chromosome, individual genotypes were joined using CombineGVCFs with convert-to-base-pair-resolution, and the GenotypeGVCFs tool was then applied to include nonvariant sites. Finally, for each individual, the whole dataset split by chromosome was concatenated with bcftools concat (bcftools, RRID:SCR_ 005227), keeping only the autosomes. Then, for each sample, we used the raw dataset to calculate average genome heterozygosity. We generated nonoverlapping sliding windows for each of the reference genomes and included only sites (both variant and invariant) with site quality >30 (QUAL field in a VCF file from GATK). Only windows containing more than 60,000 unfiltered sites were considered. Visualization was carried out with ggplot2 (RRID:SCR_ 014601) in R v.4.4.2.
Results and Discussion
Genome assembly and annotation

We generated a high-quality chromosome-level assembly for C. gasperettii by combining PacBio HiFi (65 Gbp of data), Hi-C (96 Gbp of data), and Illumina data (135 Gbp of data) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. S3). First, we de novo assembled the HiFi reads into 1,018 contigs (N50 = 45.7 Mbp; longest contig: 149.99 Mbp). Then, using the proximity ligation data (i.e., Hi-C), we scaffolded the genome into 319 scaffolds (N50 = 111.38 Mbp; largest scaffold: 345.38 Mbp). After manual curation, the scaffolding parameters of our genome were improved (N50 = 214.14 Mbp; largest scaffold: 361.99 Mbp), containing 99.44% of the genome present in 19 scaffolds or pseudochromosomes (7 macro-, 10 micro-, Z and W sex chromosomes; Table 1 and Fig. 1B). The total genome length was 1.63 Gb, similar to other venomous snakes (Table 1), with a contig N50 of 45.6 Mbp, ~3.3 times more contiguous than the N. naja genome, ~228 times more contiguous than the A. sagrei genome, but 0.67 times less contiguous than the recently published C. adamanteus genome, making it one of the most contiguous chromosomal squamate genomes assembled to date (Table 1). We assessed the completeness of the assembly using BUSCO with the sauropsida gene set (n = 7,480). Upon evaluation, we successfully identified 92.8% of the genes (91.4% single-copy, 1.4% duplicated), while the remaining genes were fragmented (1%) or missing (6.2%; Fig. 1). For the de novo assembly, GC content and repeat content were 37.87% and 43.63%, respectively. The repetitive landscape was dominated by retroelements (30.25%), with a majority of LINEs (21.25%) (Supplementary Table S3). Finally, we annotated 27,158 different protein-coding genes within our assembly, with a total of 194 putative toxins or toxin-paralog genes. Toxin genes were found in both macro- and microchromosomes (Fig. 1), and were found on individual contigs. Finally, we also found a battery of 3FTxs and myotoxin-like genes, but they were not represented in our proteome and RNA-seq dataset (see below).

Genomic architecture highly conserved among vipers

Whole-genome synteny comparisons showed similarity between C. gasperettii and C. adamanteus, with large syntenic blocks both within macro- and microchromosomes (Fig. 2). Some chromosomal rearrangements were observed between viperids and elapids, as previously discussed by, with a fission of chromosome 4 in N. naja to form chromosomes 5 and 7 in vipers, and a fusion of chromosomes 5 and 6 in N. naja to form chromosome 4 in vipers. Interestingly, several chromosomal rearrangements between lizards and snakes have occurred: we found several fission events in the A. sagrei genome, including one fission from chromosome 2 that originates the current Z chromosome in snakes (Fig. 2).

The 4 smallest scaffolds (14, 15, 16, and 17) of A. sagrei were removed because no orthologous groups were found with other species. Toxins uniquely expressed in the venom glands

Our analyses of multitissue transcriptomic data (23 samples from 2 individuals covering 13 different tissues) reported a total of 23,178 expressed genes (TPM > 1). A heatmap of the 2,000 most variable genes reported unique upregulated genes for each of the analyzed tissues (Supplementary Fig. S5). The venom gland transcriptome contained a total of 7,237 genes expressed (TPM > 500), including a total of 65 putative toxin genes. From those, we did not detect any 3FTxs and/or myotoxin-like gene transcripts. Differential gene expression analyses revealed a total of 161 genes (33 putative toxin genes) that were differentially upregulated (FC > 2 and 1% false discovery rate) in venom glands compared to other tissues (Fig. 3A and Supplementary Figs S6 and S7). Finally, a total of 10 toxin genes (CRISP2, SVMP9, SVMP10, SVSP8, SVSP7, SVSP5, CTL14, CTL15, SVSP4, and SVMP13) were uniquely expressed in the venom gland, encoding for the minimal core venom effector (Fig. 3A), and in line with the main toxins found within the proteome (Fig. 3B), although some differences were observed (such as the absence of PLA2 within the highly expressed genes), possibly due to individual venom differences. These 10 genes, together with other SVMPs, SVSPs, and C-type lectins (CTLs), were highly expressed in the venom gland and form the core toxic effector components of the venom. Targeting the core toxins together with other well-known modulators of venom may help manufacture of synthetic antivenom treatments and improve neutralization tests of current antivenoms. However, more transcriptomic data should be incorporated to correct for potential ontogenetic and geographical variation in venom composition in C. gasperettii.

SVSPs and SVMPs as main toxins

Venom proteomics identified SVSPs and SVMPs as the most abundant toxin families within the venom of C. gasperettii, with 37.38% and 22.19% of the venom being composed by peptides from those 2 families, respectively (Fig. 3B); the dominance of these 2 toxin families is consistent with previous research on the same genus. Other toxin families identified were DISI (12.74%), CTL (7.25%), PLA2 (5.47%), cysteine-rich secretory proteins (CRISP; 4.34%) or L-amino acid oxidase (LAAO; 1.71%) (Fig. 3B). We did not detect any 3FTx or myotoxin-like peptides within the proteome.
SVMPs

We analyzed the evolution of venom of the most abundant venom toxin groups (i.e., SVMPs and SVSPs, as well as PLA2). After a thorough manual curation, we used comparative genomics to evaluate the number and position of those genes in comparison with the Indian cobra (N. naja), the Eastern diamondback rattlesnake (C. adamanteus), and Fea's viper (Azemiops feae). We reported a total of 13 fully contiguous tandem array SVMPs for C. gasperettii (Fig. 4A), next to the nontoxic paralogous gene ADAM28 and flanked by the NEFL and NEFM nontoxic genes. Microsyntenic analyses showed gene copy number variation between the studied species (Fig. 4A). Overall, we can see an expansion in the number of SVMPs within the Viperidae family, particurlarly in C. adamanteus (22 copies unique to vipers and 10 lineage-specific copies) but also in C. gasperettii (12 copies unique to vipers and 1 lineage-specific copy) (Fig. 4A). Then, we reconstructed the evolutionary history of this toxin family (Figs 4B and Supplementary Fig. S8). Phylogenetic analyses for this toxin group reported a highly supported clade comprising ADAM28 peptides, the nontoxic paralogous gene. The second clade of orthologous toxin-peptides were found within both elapid and viperid families (including species from Crotalinae and Viperinae subfamilies in viperids; Supplementary Fig. S8) as well as 2 SVMPs from A. feae. Interestingly, we report a new toxin-coding gene within C. gasperettii with a different evolutionary history, as it did not share orthology with any other gene (Fig. 4B). This new gene likely arose from a duplication event of SVMP13, within the group of SVMP MDC1 toxins (Supplementary Fig. S8). Our discovery of a novel SVMP gene in C. gasperettii adds to the growing body of work on the dynamic evolution of venom systems. Similar gene expansions and duplications have been observed in other species, such as PLA2 toxin-coding genes found in the venom of A. feae, highlighting the lineage-specific nature of venom evolution. The gene we identified, possibly arising from an SVMP13 duplication, does not share orthology with genes in other species, suggesting the presence of hidden toxin diversity in venom systems. This discovery highlights the importance of using genomics in studying venom evolution, as this putatively toxic gene was not found to be differentially upregulated in the venom gland or recovered in the proteome (Fig. 3). More genomic data will indicate if SVMP12 is unique for the Viperinae subfamily, the Cerastes genus, or if it is only found in C. gasperettii. All other clades were unique to viperids (and some exclusive only to crotalids), except for a clade composed by SVMPs unique to elapids, as previously discussed in. Interestingly, one of the toxins (SVMP8) was not a class P-III SVMP, as it clusters within the MAD-4/5 clade (class P-II SVMP), contrary to the proteomic results where all SVMPs were categorized within the class P-III (Fig. 3B). Although there has been a clear expansion of the SVMP family within the Crotalus genus, our results suggest that the origin of that expansion was at the beginning of the Viperidae family, as most of the groups are also present within the Viperinae subfamily.

PLA2

Regarding PLA2, we report 2 tandem repeat venom genes for C. gasperettii within the non-toxic PLA2-g2E and PLA2-g2F array (Fig. 4C), flanked by OTUD3 and MUL1 nontoxic genes, as previously reported in other species. The number of venomous PLA2s in C. gasperettii was lower than in A. feae and C. adamanteus. Phylogenetic results for PLA2 genes showed a fully supported clade containing both nontoxic PLA2-g2E and PLA2-g2F as outgroups (Fig. 4D and Supplementary Fig. S9). We also found all other PLA2 groups reported in previous studies: PLA2-gC, PLA2-gK, PLA2-gB, PLA2-gD, and PLA2-gA. The 2 genes for our target species clustered in different groups (Fig. 4D and Supplementary Fig. S9). The first PLA2 was a PLA2-gD, which is a group of PLA2s exclusively found in true vipers (subfamily Viperinae). The second one was a PLA2-gC which is more ancestral as it is also found in other pitvipers and nonvenomous snakes such as pythons. The genomic results are consistent with the proteomics, indicating that specific duplications of PLA2 toxin-coding genes have not occurred in C. gasperettii.
SVSPs

We found 8 different SVSPs within the genome of C. gasperettii, flanked by RBM42 and GRAMD1A nontoxic genes (Fig. 4E). For this toxin family, we were only able to compare the results with C. adamanteus. We were unable to confidently determine the location of SVSPs in the N. naja genome (several regions matched our venomous SVSP genes as well as the flanking genes). Moreover, A. feae was also not compared because SVSPs were not assembled in a single contig. Phylogenetic results showed 3 clades, with 2 containing C. gasperettii genes (Fig. 4F and Supplementary Fig. S10). Group 1 was mainly present within Crotalus, although there was the presence of some true vipers species, but not in C. gasperettii (Fig. S10). Group 2 contained 6 genes within C. adamanteus and only 2 for C. gasperettii. Interestingly, Group 3 was expanded in C. gasperettii (Fig. 4E) with a total of 6 copies, while 4 were found within C. adamanteus. Most of the toxins included in the analyses for true vipers were also found in Group 3 (Supplementary Fig. S10), indicating a possible expansion of this group of toxins in true vipers (or gene losses in pit vipers). Overall, our high-quality chromosome-level reference genome has shed light on the evolution of the main toxin-coding gene families, indicating a compelling correlation between the abundance of toxin-coding genes and the prevalence of these toxins in the venom of C. gasperettii.
Glacial periods drove population expansions of C. gasperettii

The Arabian horned viper (C. gasperettii) is a widespread species, categorized as "Least Concern" by the IUCN. Genome-wide diversity was in line with its conservation status, as it showed similar heterozygosity levels compared to other venomous snakes (Fig. 5A). However, more individuals should be sampled along its distribution to verify that similar heterozygosity levels are found across its range. PSMC analyses showed several population expansions and contractions in the last 400 kya, whilst the effective population size of C. gasperettii remained relatively constant from 1 until 10 Mya (Fig. 5B). Interestingly, population expansions were coincident with the last glacial and penultimate glacial periods (gray lines on Fig. 5B), with a large population increase during the penultimate glacial period (1.94-1.35 mya) (Fig. 5B). In fact, during glacial periods, the global sea level dropped around 150 m, exposing the floor and the sand to the wind, which promoted aridification in the Arabian Peninsula and potentially increased habitat suitability for the species. PSMC results may vary depending on the generation time as well as the mutational rate specified. The absence of species-specific data for this analyses may bias our results, although it is a general consensus in the literature when inferring demographic analyses such as ours in snakes (e.g.,).

Conclusions

Our high-quality chromosome-level reference genome for C. gasperettii showed that chromosomal architecture is highly conserved between Crotalinae and Viperinae subfamilies, and differs from elapid genomes by a small number of chromosomal rearrangements. We also found the genomic coordinates of the main toxin-encoding genes, highlighting gene duplication as the main driver in the evolution of SVMP and SVSP toxins. We identified a new SVMP toxin-coding gene, showcasing the importance of using high-quality reference genomes (combined with other -omic techniques) for thoroughly characterizing toxin-encoding genes. Finally, this is a new and important resource for a large clade with few reference genomes available. Future genomic studies focusing on Old World viper evolution will benefit greatly from this resource, which will help unveil the origin and diversification of venom and serve as an essential genomic tool for further venomic studies on the subfamily Viperinae.

passages.text: Enhanced absorption in organic solar cells via combined anti-reflection and Mie resonance effects in subwavelength ellipsoidal dielectric nanostructures

This study presents subwavelength ellipsoidal dielectric nanostructures (SEDNs) to enhance absorption in organic solar cells (OSCs) through the combined effects of broadband anti-reflection (AR) and Mie scattering. Strong forward-directed scattering at shorter wavelengths is produced by the simultaneous excitation of both electric and magnetic moments in the SEDN, thereby lengthening the optical path length inside the active layer. Additionally, the SEDNs reduce reflection over a broad wavelength range, further enhancing absorption. By fine-tuning the structural parameters of the SEDN, including a minor axis diameter of 100 nm, a spacing of 30 nm, and an aspect ratio of 3.6 for TE polarization, a short-circuit current density (JSC) of 28.11 mA/cm2 is achieved, representing an 9.46% improvement over planar OSCs. Light scattering is analyzed through multipolar decomposition, while the AR effect is studied using optical admittance analysis. The proposed approaches not only offer performance enhancements for applications such as thin-film solar cells, photodetectors, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces, but also show potential for polarization-sensitive applications including bio-imaging, defect analysis, and optical security systems.

Introduction

Organic solar cells (OSCs) have attracted considerable interest for their potential to enable low-cost energy conversion due to advantages such as low material costs, solution-based processing, low-temperature fabrication, and simple device architecture. Recent progress in the OSCs has led to significant efficiency improvements, with power conversion efficiency (PCE) reaching over 19% for single-junction devices and more than 20% for tandem structures. These advancements stem from breakthroughs such as the development of novel materials for active layers and interfaces, optimization of device architecture and metal contact configurations, reduction of structural and morphological defects, and the incorporation of optical spacers.

However, due to the low mobility and high recombination rates of photogenerated charge carriers in organic materials, the active layer must remain thin to ensure efficient charge transport and minimize recombination losses. This thin active layer leads to significant optical losses due to insufficient light absorption, which continues to be a major limitation in the OSCs. In bulk heterojunction organic solar cells, which utilize a blend of n-type acceptors and p-type donors, the optimal active layer thickness, balancing optical interference and recombination losses, ranges from 80 nm to 120 nm. Despite the high absorption coefficient of the organic materials, a layer of this thickness is still insufficient to absorb all incident light, resulting in losses. Addressing the challenge of inefficient light absorption in thin active layers remains crucial for increasing photocurrent and further enhancing PCE.

This challenge underscores the importance of light trapping (LT) mechanisms in the OSCs. Promising approaches include shaping the active layer into photonic crystal or grating structuresapplying anti-reflection coatingsand integrating plasmonic nanoresonators or dielectric Mie-resonant nanostructures. While structuring the active layer can improve LT, it also introduces difficulties, as the solution-processed layer must remain close to electrical contacts for efficient charge extraction. Additionally, structuring increases defects and impurities, leading to greater charge recombination. Plasmonic nanoresonators suffer from parasitic optical losses due to intrinsic absorption in metals, which limits their efficiency and confines absorption enhancement to a narrow spectral range, as they do not support magnetic resonances. Moreover, when embedded near the photoactive layer, metallic nanoparticles can introduce additional electrical losses by increasing charge carrier recombination. In contrast, dielectric nanostructures based on Mie resonances can simultaneously support electric and magnetic modes, enabling broadband absorption across the solar spectrum. These dielectric structures also minimize electrical losses, as they are typically placed on top of the transparent electrode rather than being embedded within the active region. Multiple Mie resonances in these structures enhance light scattering, effectively increasing the optical path length within the active layer. However, while such nanostructures can be fabricated using techniques such as nanoimprinting, self-assembly, or lithographychallenges remain in achieving large-area and precisely periodic arrangements, which limit their scalability for practical device integration.

This study explores the combined effects of broadband anti-reflection (AR) and Mie scattering to enhance absorption in the OSCs using subwavelength ellipsoidal dielectric nanostructures (SEDNs). Simultaneous excitation of electric and magnetic moments in the SEDN array generates strong forward-directed light scattering at shorter wavelengths, thereby extending the optical path length within the active layer. Moreover, the SEDNs reduce reflection over a broad range of wavelengths, further boosting absorption. After optimizing the geometrical parameters of the SEDNs, we attain a short-circuit current density (JSC) of 28.11 mA/cm2, reflecting a 9.5% improvement over planar OSCs. We also investigate how the polarization angle of incident light influences absorption enhancement and analyze the scattering behavior through multipolar resonances and the AR effect using optical admittance analysis.
Results and discussion

Schematic of a planar organic solar cell (OSC) incorporating an array of subwavelength ellipsoidal dielectric nanostructures (SEDNs) to enhance light trapping (LT) and anti-reflection (AR) performance.

Figure 1 depicts the structure of a bulk heterojunction OSC based on PM6:Y6, integrated with the SEDN. The SEDN is defined by three key parameters, including the minor axis diameter (D), the spacing (S), and the aspect ratio (ASP), which is the ratio of D to the major axis diameter (L). The planar OSC structure includes a transparent front electrode composed of indium tin oxide (ITO) with a thickness of 100 nm, followed by a 40 nm zinc oxide (ZnO) electron transport layer, an 80 nm PM6:Y6 active layer, a 10 nm molybdenum trioxide (MoO3) hole transport layer, and a 100 nm silver (Ag) rear electrode. This structural design of the planar OSC has been broadly used in previous studies. In the simulation, the substrate is located beneath the Ag layer, and for the actual fabrication of the solar cell, the layers are deposited in reverse order starting from the Ag layer. While ITO typically requires thermal annealing at temperatures above 300  C, the PM6:Y6 active layer is usually processed at temperatures below 200 C. One approach to address this thermal mismatch is to anneal ITO at low temperatures. Previous studies have demonstrated that ITO can be annealed at temperatures below 200  C while maintaining acceptable sheet resistance and transmittance. Although this approach enables practical fabrication of the solar cell, the performance still falls short compared to high-temperature annealing. In addition, since the SEDN is fabricated on top of the ITO after the planar solar cell is completed, it can operate without causing electrical losses. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is an excellent choice for SEDN material due to its exceptional optical properties, including a high refractive index and a negligible extinction coefficient in the visible range. These attributes are pivotal for promoting efficient scattering in the forward direction. Additionally, its high refractive index enables a reduction in feature size, boosting the AR performance of the SEDN across a broad wavelength range. Moreover, TiO2 is widely used as a UV-blocking material due to its high extinction coefficient in the ultraviolet region, making it highly resistant to UV exposure. As such, it can also serve to protect the photoactive layer from potential UV-induced degradation. TiO2 ellipsoidal nanoparticles have been explored via sol-gel method or modified solvothermal methodas well as through self-assembly at various interfaces and magnetic-field-assisted alignment. While these approaches offer promising routes toward ordered nanostructures, challenges remain in achieving high structural precision.

The ellipsoidal shape of the SEDN introduces polarization-dependent variations in light interactions with the structure, necessitating separate analyses for each polarization direction. As illustrated in the right image of Fig. 1, TM polarization refers to light with an electric field oscillating along the x-axis, while TE polarization refers to light with an electric field oscillating along the y-axis. To optimize the SEDNs for each polarization, three-dimensional (3D) finite element method (FEM) simulations are conducted using the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics. During the optimization process, the S and ASP parameters of the SEDNs are systematically varied, while the D value is kept constant. The wavelength-dependent complex refractive indices of all materials, including the photoactive layer, were obtained from previous studies. In the simulation, the refractive index of the active layer was assumed to be spatially uniform, as variations caused by non-uniform charge carrier distribution in organic semiconductors are generally negligible. TiO2 generally exhibits anisotropic refractive indices depending on its crystalline phase. In this study, we used refractive index values obtained from previous workwhere TiO2 films were deposited as amorphous state and could transition to the anatase phase depending on the deposition temperature. Since the anatase phase exhibits only weak optical anisotropy, with refractive index differences between crystallographic directions typically less than 0.1, we treated TiO2 as having an isotropic refractive index in our calculations. After determining the optimal geometrical parameters of the SEDN that yield the highest JSC for both TM and TE polarizations, we examine the optical properties of the SEDN with these optimized parameters for a specific polarization. Our focus is primarily on examining the optical properties of OSCs integrated with the SEDN optimized for its geometrical parameters, rather than their electrical transport properties. This evaluation is achieved by calculating the absorption within the active layer and subsequently determining the JSC using Eq. (1)..

where e represents the elementary charge, h indicates Planck's constant, c stands for the speed of light in a vacuum, lambda denotes the wavelength, and IAM1.5 (lambda) represents the solar spectral irradiance under air mass 1.5 conditions. We assumed 100% internal quantum efficiency (IQE) in this study to focus on the optical effects and the resulting enhancement in absorption. In this context, the quantum efficiency spectrum corresponds directly to the absorption spectrum within the active layer (Abs(lambda)). In real devices, however, electrical losses such as exciton recombination and charge carrier transport limitations may occur, which can reduce the IQE. Nevertheless, such electrical effects are independent of the optical absorption itself and may result in a slight decrease in the JSC. A more detailed analysis that includes electrical simulations will be addressed in a future study.
JSC as a function of spacing (S) and aspect ratio (ASP) for the SEDN, with fixed minor axis diameters (D) of (a) 80 nm, (b) 100 nm, (c) 120 nm, and (d) 140 nm, under TM polarization.

Initially, a spherical structure with an ASP of 1 is used to investigate changes in JSC as a function of D and S, as depicted in Figure S1. The maximum JSC is 27.2 mA/cm2, occurring at D = 180 nm and S = 160 nm. Using this result as a foundation, the shape of the SEDN is optimized by adjusting S and ASP, with the previously identified optimal D (180 nm) serving as the baseline. This analysis reveals that an ellipsoidal shape yields the highest JSC. The parameter D is further examined in increments of 20 nm. Figure S2 presents 2D contour plots of JSC as a function of S and ASP for fixed D values of 160, 180, and 200 nm under TM polarization. Figure 2 illustrates the dependence of JSC on S and ASP of the SEDN under TM-polarized light, with D held constant. As shown in Figs. 2 (a) - (d), the highest JSC values achieved for D = 80, 100, 120, and 140 nm are 27.92 mA/cm2 (S = 50 nm, ASP = 2.8), 27.97 mA/cm2 (S = 70 nm, ASP = 2.2), 27.74 mA/cm2 (S = 90 nm, ASP = 1.8), and 27.58 mA/cm2 (S = 260 nm, ASP = 1.8), respectively. When compared to the planar OSC (25.68 mA/cm2), these JSC values represent enhancement rates of 8.7%, 8.9%, 8.0%, and 7.4%, respectively. The fine-tuned structural parameters for the SEDN under TM polarization are found at D = 100 nm, S = 70 nm, and ASP = 2.2.
JSC as a function of spacing (S) and aspect ratio (ASP) for the SEDN, with fixed minor axis diameters (D) of (a) 80 nm, (b) 100 nm, (c) 120 nm, and (d) 140 nm, under TE polarization.

For TE-polarized light incident on the SEDN, the optimization process also begins with a starting point of D = 180 nm, derived from the spherical configuration. Figure S3 provides 2D contour plots illustrating JSC as a function of S and ASP for fixed D values of 160, 180, and 200 nm under TE polarization. In Figs. 3 (a) - (d), the variation of JSC with S and ASP is shown for TE-polarized light incident on the SEDNs at fixed D values of 80, 100, 120, and 140 nm. The maximum JSC values are 28.01 mA/cm2 (S = 20 nm, ASP = 4.4) for D = 80 nm, 28.11 mA/cm2 (S = 30 nm, ASP = 3.6) for D = 100 nm, 27.93 mA/cm2 (S = 50 nm, ASP = 3) for D = 120 nm, and 27.54 mA/cm2 (S = 140 nm, ASP = 2.4) for D = 140 nm. These correspond to enhancement rates of 9.1%, 9.5%, 8.8%, and 7.2%, respectively, compared to the flat OSC. Thus, the optimal SEDN parameters for TE polarization, as identified through the optimization process depicted in Fig. 3, are D = 100 nm, S = 30 nm, and ASP = 3.6. We note that while the optimal geometric parameters may vary slightly depending on the structure or refractive index of the solar cell's active layer, the same optimization process can be applied to enhance its optical absorption efficiency.

(a) Absorption spectra in PM6:Y6 of planar OSCs with and without the SEDNs under TM polarization at D = 100 nm, S = 70 nm, and ASP = 2.2, and under TE polarization at D = 100 nm, S = 30 nm, and ASP = 3.6. (b) JSC as a function of PM6:Y6 thickness for the planar OSC compared to OSCs integrated with the SEDNs optimized for TM and TE polarizations.

Figure 4 (a) presents the simulated absorption spectra in the PM6:Y6 active layer of a planar OSC (black) and OSCs integrated with the SEDNs optimized for TM (red) and TE (blue) polarizations. The planar OSC exhibits Fabry-Perot resonance-induced absorption peaks at wavelengths of 400, 560, 660, and 820 nm, with corresponding valleys at wavelengths of 450, 610, and 740 nm. Integration of the SEDNs enhances absorption at wavelengths of 440, 620, and 750 nm for both polarizations, driven by LT and AR effects, which are investigated later. The TE-optimized SEDN (SEDNTE) slightly outperforms the TM-optimized counterpart (SEDNTM) in absorption over the range 380-480 nm, contributing to a higher overall performance. Figure 4 (b) illustrates the variation in JSC of the planar OSC as a function of the PM6:Y6 active layer thickness, alongside the JSC values achieved with the SEDNs optimized for TM and TE polarizations. The integration of the SEDNs enhances the JSC to 27.97 mA/cm2 for TM polarization and 28.11 mA/cm2 for TE polarization, corresponding to the JSC of a planar OSC with active layer thicknesses of 245 nm and 255 nm, respectively. Given that the bulk heterojunction OSCs typically have active layer thicknesses constrained to 80-120 nm, the LT effects enabled by the SEDN integration are significantly important in enhancing performance. This study focuses solely on optical absorption enhancement and evaluates only the JSC. Based on a previous report on PM6:Y6-based solar cells, which demonstrated an open-circuit voltage (VOC) of 0.83 V and a fill factor (FF) of 74.8%, the PCE can be estimated to use the following equation, assuming identical electrical properties..

Here, Pin refers to the input power, which is assumed to be 100 mW/cm2 under standard AM1.5G conditions. Based on this, the PCE is improved from 15.91% for the planar solar cell (JSC = 25.68 mA/cm2) to 17.45% for the solar cell incorporating the SEDNTE structure (JSC = 28.11 mA/cm2). In addition, to explore the impact of vertical alignment, we performed geometric optimization for the SEDN with the major axis aligned along the z-direction, as shown in Figure S4. The highest JSC of 27.92 mA/cm2 is achieved when D = 60 nm, S = 10 nm, and ASP = 1.4. The corresponding absorption spectrum is presented in Figure S5, alongside those of planar OSCs with and without the SEDN.

We also investigate how the polarization angle affects the absorption spectra in PM6:Y6 and the corresponding JSC in the OSCs with the SEDNTE and SEDNTM. The polarization is rotated from 0  (aligned with the x-axis) to 90 , while maintaining a constant electric field intensity at all angles. The SEDNTM structure achieves a JSC of 27.97 mA/cm2 at 0  and 27.49 mA/cm2 at 90 , while the SEDNTE structure attains 26.57 mA/cm2 at 0  and 28.11 mA/cm2 at 90 , as shown in Figure S6 (a). Figures S6 (b) and (c) present the absorption spectra at polarization angles of 0  and 90  for TM and TE polarizations, respectively. As the polarization rotates perpendicularly in each structure, the absorption changes accordingly, resulting in a variation in JSC. This occurs because the LT effect from the SEDNs reduces the electric field intensity trapped by the polarization perpendicular to the optimal structure. Figures S7 and S8 compare the absorption distributions at representative wavelengths where absorption decreases under perpendicular polarization. In addition, to investigate the effect of variations in the refractive index of TiO2 on absorption and JSC, we varied the refractive index of TiO2 from 2.1 to 2.7, which is within the commonly reported range, at a wavelength of 650 nm for both the SEDNTM and SEDNTE structures, as shown in Figure S9. Within this range, the absorption in PM6:Y6 remains nearly unchanged, and the variation in JSC is minimal, with a reduction of only approximately 0.1 mA/cm2.

To identify the wavelengths at which LT or AR effects dominate the enhanced absorption in the active layer of the OSC, the scattering characteristics of the SEDN are first examined. As the OSC with the SEDNTE exhibits the highest absorption and JSC, we focus on analyzing the properties of the SEDNTE moving forward. Figure 5 (a) presents the wavelength-dependent scattering cross-section (sigmasca) and spectral multipole resonance contributions for a single SEDNTE with D = 100 nm and ASP = 3.6 in air. Mie resonances of periodic particles analyzed using the Generalized Multiparticle Mie (GMM) theory have been reported in previous study. However, the Mie resonances in periodic particle arrays can also be understood as the convolution of the single-particle scattering response with the spatial periodicity of the structure. Therefore, in analyzing the scattering characteristics of the SEDN, we approximated the system by investigating the scattering behavior of a single SEDN element. In Mie scattering, the scattering coefficient can be expressed as an infinite series.

Here, k denotes the wavevector inside particle, a represents the radius of the particle, an corresponds to the electric resonance, bn corresponds to the magnetic resonance, and n indicates the order of the resonance. Specifically, the first-order Mie coefficients a1 and b1 correspond to electric dipole (ED) and magnetic dipole (MD) modes, respectively, while higher-order coefficients represent quadrupolar and higher multipolar contributions. Figure 5 (a) displays that the simultaneous excitation of ED and MD resonances triggers strong forward scattering at lambda = 410 nm, realizing the first Kerker effect. This forward-directed scattering increases the optical path length within the PM6:Y6 active layer, significantly enhancing absorption in the 400-500 nm range. We note that in the 300-400 nm region, a strong MD resonance leads to an increase in the scattering cross-section. However, as shown in Figure S10, TiO2 exhibits intrinsic absorption in this spectral range. As a result, despite the large scattering cross-section, no significant enhancement in the absorption of the active layer is observed, as shown in Fig. 4 (a). At lambda = 620 nm, a minor contribution from the ED resonance leads to weak scattering, providing a modest absorption boost at this wavelength. However, beyond 700 nm, the scattering effect from the SEDNTE becomes negligible, indicating that absorption enhancement in this range arises from a different mechanism. It can be observed that higher-order terms beyond the quadrupole have minimal magnitudes and are only excited at short wavelengths, resulting in a negligible impact on the overall scattering. By manipulating the multipolar resonances of the SEDN, the wavelength range for optimizing absorption and scattering direction can be tailored to specific applications. For example, enhancing backward scattering in metamaterials or creating reflective colors in solar cells can be achieved by tuning the SEDN to satisfy the second Kerker condition at targeted wavelengths. Conversely, for applications such as thin-film solar cells, photodiodes, or sensors, maximizing absorption at desired wavelengths can be achieved by adjusting the structural parameters of the SEDN to fulfill the first Kerker condition, enabling strong forward scattering.

The direction of light scattering from a scatterer is affected by the interaction between electric and magnetic fields induced by multipolar response. To quantify the propagation direction of the scattered light, the asymmetry parameter (g), which represents the scattering directionality, is determined using Eq. (7):.

where Isca denotes the intensity of the scattered light, and  indicates the cosine of the angle between the incident and scattered light directions. Figure 5 (b) exhibits the spectral asymmetry parameter for the single SEDNTE with D = 100 nm and ASP = 3.6, showing g values exceeding 0.2 across the wavelength range of 370 nm to 510 nm, with a peak value of 0.56 at lambda = 390 nm. This result indicates that the majority of the incident energy is scattered forward within these wavelengths. The pronounced forward scattering in the shorter wavelength range plays a key role in boosting the absorption efficiency of the PM6:Y6 active layer. Although the g values beyond 510 nm are above 0, suggesting forward-directional scattering, the multipoles' contributions are negligible, as shown in Fig. 5 (a). This suggests that scattering does not contribute to enhanced absorption in the active layer at longer wavelengths.

The improved absorption at longer wavelengths is analyzed by examining the AR properties of the SEDNTE. Using the effective medium approximation (EMA), the SEDNTE is represented as a single layer with an effective refractive index. For the EMA models, the choice among the linear model, the Bruggeman model, and the Maxwell-Garnett model largely depends on the specific characteristics of the material system and application. The linear model is particularly well-suited for scenarios where the transition between material phases or shapes occurs gradually, ensuring a smooth variation in properties. On the other hand, the Bruggeman model is frequently employed when the mixture of constituent materials is balanced. In contrast, the Maxwell-Garnett model is ideal for cases involving dispersed systems with very small inclusions, where the properties of the host material significantly influence the behavior of the embedded particles. Each model offers distinct advantages tailored to different structural or compositional contexts, making them versatile tools in modeling optical material properties. In the case of the SEDNTE, the volume fraction of TiO2 nanoparticles surpasses 37%, indicating that the Bruggeman model is the best choice for accurately describing the properties of the SEDNTE. The effective refractive indices of the SEDNTE are determined to be 1.46 and 1.44 at wavelengths of 620 nm and 750 nm, respectively. Figure 6 (a) presents a comparison of the reflectance of a planar OSC with the SEDNTE, calculated using both FEM (COMSOL) simulations and the Bruggeman model-based EMA. Both approaches show that integrating the SEDNTE into the planar OSC reduces reflectance at wavelengths of 440, 620, and 750 nm, thereby improving light absorption within the active layer. Notably, at shorter wavelengths of 420 nm and 620 nm, light scattering also occurs, a phenomenon not captured by the EMA model, leading to slightly higher reflectance in these regions. At longer wavelengths exceeding 700 nm, the absorption enhancement is primarily attributed to the AR effect of the SEDNTE, highlighting their effectiveness in minimizing light losses.

To gain deeper insights into the AR properties of the SEDNTE, an optical admittance analysis is performed. Optical admittance, defined as the reciprocal of optical impedance, provides a practical framework for understanding the optical behavior of materials and is widely applied in analyzing thin-film optics. It is expressed as the ratio of the electric field to the magnetic field within a material and can be mathematically represented as , where E and H represent the electric and magnetic fields, respectively, and  and  denote the permeability and permittivity. For non-magnetic materials in the optical wavelength range, permeability  is approximately 1, simplifying the optical admittance to the square root of the permittivity, effectively equating it to the complex refractive index. The surface admittance of a thin film, a critical parameter for evaluating its optical response, can be derived using the transfer matrix method, as detailed in prior research. Figures 6 (b) and (c) illustrate the admittance diagrams of the OSC incorporating the SEDNTE at wavelengths of 620 nm and 750 nm, respectively. These diagrams begin at the Ag layer, depicted as a black circle, and progress sequentially through the layers: MoO3 (black line), PM6:Y6 (red line), ZnO (blue line), and ITO (magenta line). The path concludes at the termination point of the planar OSC, marked by a black square, before extending into the SEDNTE as modeled by the EMA, ultimately ending at the SEDNTE termination point, represented by a black triangle. The reflectance is calculated from these admittance values using the formula provided in Eq. (9), allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of the AR performance of the SEDNTE..

where,  and  represent the admittance of air and final admittance, respectively. At lambda = 620 nm, the planar OSC exhibits a final admittance of (1.64, - 0.07), with a reflectance of 6%, while at lambda = 750 nm, the admittance shifts to (1.76, - 0.86), corresponding to a higher reflectance of 15.9%. In contrast, when the SEDNTE is integrated into the OSC, the final admittance values are significantly closer to that of air (1, 0), measuring (1.29, 0.03) at lambda = 620 nm and (0.83, 0.12) at lambda = 750 nm. Reflectance is drastically reduced in this configuration, dropping to 1.6% and 1.3% at wavelengths of 620 nm and 750 nm, respectively. These results highlight the effectiveness of the SEDNTE in reducing reflectance and enhancing light absorption within the active layer, particularly in the longer wavelength range, primarily due to its AR properties.

Figure 7 highlights the absorption distributions of the planar OSC and the OSC integrated with the SEDNTE at wavelengths of 440, 620, and 750 nm, while also illustrating the energy flow through Poynting vectors. The formula  is used to calculate the absorption rate per unit volume within each layer, where  is the angular frequency,  denotes the imaginary part of the permittivity, and  stands for the intensity of the electric field. To calculate the total absorption at each wavelength,  is normalized by the intensity of incident light to yield the absorption density , followed by a volume integration. Figures 7 (a) and (b) exhibit that integrating the SEDNTE enhances light scattering through contributions from ED and MD resonances, leading to a significant concentration of the electric field within the PM6:Y6 active layer. The Poynting vectors reveal that light is directed toward the central region of the PM6:Y6 at lambda = 440 nm, while scattering occurs more prominently toward the edges of the active layer at lambda = 620 nm. This scattering effect is amplified by the periodic arrangement of the SEDNTE, which effectively redistributes light within the PM6:Y6 layer at these wavelengths. Conversely, as shown in Fig. 7 (c), the behavior at lambda = 750 nm is markedly different. Scattering effects are minimal, and the Poynting vectors indicate that the SEDNTE has little impact on the energy flow. As discussed earlier, the enhanced absorption at longer wavelengths is primarily due to the AR properties of the SEDNTE, which reduce reflectance and optimize LT within the device.

Figures 8 (a) and (b) present 2D contour maps of the absorption spectra in the active layer as a function of incident angle for TM and TE polarizations, respectively, in OSCs integrated with the SEDNTE structure. Figure 8 (c) shows the corresponding variation of JSC with incident angle, derived from the absorption characteristics of each polarization. As previously shown in Figure S6, the SEDNTE structure under TM polarization yields a lower JSC of 26.57 mA/cm2 due to a weaker LT effect compared to TE polarization. For TM polarization, the absorption peak is maintained up to an incident angle of 60 , resulting in only a slight decrease in JSC. However, at larger angles, the absorption peak diminishes rapidly, leading to a sharp decline in JSC. In contrast, for TE polarization, the absorption peak is preserved up to approximately 70 , allowing JSC to remain as high as 23.34 mA/cm2 even at this angle.
Methods

To address the mathematical complexity of space- and time-dependent physical phenomena, researchers have developed a wide range of numerical approaches for solving the corresponding partial differential equations (PDEs). Since analytical solutions are rarely feasible for such equations, discretization methods are essential for numerical analysis. Over the years, various techniques, including the finite difference method (FDM), finite element method (FEM), spacetime Fourier modal method (ST-FMM), and rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), have been employed to model and simulate these systems. In addition, machine learning-based optimization strategies have gained popularity for improving computational efficiency and guiding design exploration. The adoption of these methods has significantly advanced the simulation of complex physical systems across multiple domains.

Among these methods, the FEM is particularly well-suited for simulating complex nanostructures and solving multiphysics problems involving optics and electromagnetics. In this study, three-dimensional FEM simulations were performed using COMSOL to investigate the optical characteristics of the system. Although this work focuses on optical behavior, the simulation framework is designed to be extendable to future electrical analyses, including carrier transport and doping effects. The SEDN structure was divided into finely meshed elements with varying shapes to numerically solve Maxwell's equations within each region. To suppress unwanted reflections at the boundaries, perfectly matched layers (PMLs) were incorporated at the upper and lower boundaries of the solar cell model, while the x and y axes were set with periodic boundary conditions to simulate a single SEDN unit within a repeating structure. The mesh resolution was carefully chosen, with the thickness of each element set to one-third of the smallest structural dimension, ensuring precise modeling of the geometry.

The absorption efficiency was evaluated by calculating the power dissipation density within the active layer and integrating it over the entire volume. The absorption data were used to estimate JSC under the assumption of perfect carrier collection, corresponding to an internal quantum efficiency of 100%. JSC was derived using Eq. (1) and was further refined by integrating the active layer absorption weighted by the AM1.5 solar spectrum over the 300-1000 nm wavelength range.

To analyze the light scattering properties of the SEDN, an external electric field was applied to an individual SEDN. Key optical parameters, including the total scattering cross-section and multipolar spectra, were calculated using Eqs. (2)-(6). Additionally, the asymmetry parameter, derived using Eq. (7), was used to quantify the directional scattering behavior of the SEDN.

For the AR analysis, the SEDN was treated as an effective single layer with a refractive index approximated using the Bruggeman model-based EMA. Reflectance based on this approximation was compared to results from FEM simulations to validate the AR performance. Furthermore, the admittance diagrams were employed to visualize and compare the optical performance of planar OSCs and those integrated with the SEDN, focusing on the admittance trajectories and endpoints to confirm the enhanced AR functionality of the SEDN.
Conclusion

In conclusion, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of ellipsoidal dielectric nanostructures designed at subwavelength scales to improve light absorption in the OSCs. These nanostructures employ a dual mechanism, combining broadband AR properties with efficient Mie scattering, resulting in enhanced LT within the active layer. The simultaneous excitation of both electric and magnetic resonances within the nanostructures induces pronounced forward scattering, particularly at shorter wavelengths, effectively increasing the optical path length. Additionally, the AR effect of these nanostructures reduces surface reflections over a broad spectrum, further boosting absorption. Through optimization, the OSC integrated with the SEDN featuring a D of 100 nm, an S of 30 nm, and an ASP of 3.6 achieves a JSC of 28.11 mA/cm2, representing a 9.5% improvement over planar OSCs. These findings highlight the broad applicability of the proposed design strategy, offering performance improvements in devices such as photodiodes, absorbers, sensors, and metasurfaces, while its polarization sensitivity further enables applications in polarization-resolved technologies including bio-imaging, defect inspection, and optical security. The proposed SEDN exhibits strong optical advantages and application potential. While fabrication is possible via interfacial or magnetically guided self-assembly, ensuring high structural precision remains a key challenge.

passages.text: Metabolic markers detect early ostedifferentiation of mesenchymal stem cells from multiple donors
Background

Mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) are pivotal bioengineering tools, offering significant promise for applications in bone regeneration. However, their therapeutic potential is limited by inter-donor variability and experimental issues. This study aimed to identify robust metabolic markers of osteodifferentiation applicable across multiple donors, while providing insight into the metabolic pathways actively involved in the process.
Methods

Untargeted nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomics was applied to characterize the intra- and extracellular metabolic adaptations of human adipose-derived MSC (hAMSC) undergoing osteogenic differentiation, compared to proliferation alone. Multivariate and univariate statistical analysis was carried out on data from three independent donors, and cross-validation was employed to evaluate the predictive capacity of the proposed markers.
Results

Variations in the levels of selected (nine) intracellular and (seventeen) extracellular metabolites detect osteodifferentiation by day 7 (out of 21), with nearly 100% accuracy. These signatures suggest a metabolic shift from glycolysis/OxPhos to lactic fermentation, fatty acid beta-oxidation and phosphocreatine hydrolysis. Intracellular glucose, lactate, citrate and specific amino acids are redirected towards protein synthesis and glycosylation, with some of the secreted metabolites (e.g., citrate) seemingly involved in biomineralization and other extracellular roles. Membrane metabolism, antioxidant mechanisms and adenosine metabolism are also impacted by osteodifferentiation.
Conclusions

These findings reveal effective donor-independent markers of hAMSC osteodifferentiation, with a robust extracellular signature standing out for potential rapid and non-invasive detection of osteocommitted cells.
