BM: breast muscle. LM: leg muscle.
Figure 1

Quality Control of the Metabolomes of Muscle Samples. A total of 1,516 and 1,503 metabolites were identified in breast and leg muscles, respectively, under negative and positive ion modes. Principal component analysis revealed overlapping metabolic profiles among breast and leg muscles across different age groups, suggesting the presence of common metabolite modes (Figure 1A, B). Partial least squares discriminant analysis further clarified the differentiation among groups. Notably, breast muscle samples exhibited clear separation among CR4, CR6, and CR8 (Figure 1C), whereas leg muscles showed overlap between CR6_LM and CR8_LM, indicating fewer metabolic differences at these two ages (Figure 1D). The 200-permutation test confirmed the robustness of the PLS-DA model, demonstrating a low risk of overfitting (Figure 1E, F).

Screening and comparative analysis of differential metabolites. Upset diagrams were used in total differential metabolites in the BM (A) and LM (B), respectively. The variable importance in projection (VIP) analysis were used in the top 20 differentially metabolites (DMs) in the BM (C) and LM (D) from Lueyang black-bone chickens at different ages.
Figure 2

Screening and Comparative Analysis of Differential Metabolites. A total of 512 and 408 differential metabolites were identified in the breast and leg muscles, respectively. Specifically, 343, 414, and 89 DMs were identified in comparisons of CR4_BM vs. CR6_BM, CR4_BM vs. CR8_BM, and CR6_BM vs. CR8_BM, respectively. Thirteen metabolites were common across all comparisons, including tryptophol, palmitoylcarnitine, and L-proline (Figure 2A).

Similarly, in the leg muscles, 302, 378, and 51 DMs were identified in CR4_LM vs. CR6_LM, CR4_LM vs. CR8_LM, and CR6_LM vs. CR8_LM, respectively. Ten shared metabolites were observed among all groups, including guanosine diphosphate and isopropylmaleate (Figure 2B). The number of DMs between CR6 and CR8 was relatively low in both muscle types, indicating metabolic stabilization in chickens older than six months.

Further analysis of the top 20 DMs revealed significant metabolic shifts. In breast muscles, 8'-hydroxyabscisate, docosanedioate, and 9,12,13-TriHOME decreased with age, while 5-hydroxyhexadenoylcarnitine and LysoPI (0:0/18:0) accumulated in CR8 (Figure 2C). In leg muscles, amino acids and peptides such as Leu-Ala-His and Met-Phe were enriched in CR4, while phospholipids and lipid metabolites showed an increase in CR8 (Figure 2D). These findings suggest that metabolic alterations were closely linked to muscle composition changes in Lueyang black-bone chickens.
KEGG enrichment analysis of DMs in BM(A-C) and LM (D-F) from Lueyang black-bone chickens at different ages.
Figure 3

Cluster Analysis of the Differential Metabolites. HMDB compound classification indicated that the DMs were primarily organic acids, lipids, organoheterocyclic compounds, and organic oxygen compounds (Figure S1). KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that in breast muscles, DMs in CR4_BM vs. CR6_BM and CR4_BM vs. CR8_BM, were mainly enriched in amino acid metabolism, including phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis; as well as aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis (Figure 3A, B). In CR6_BM vs. CR8_BM, DMs were mainly enriched in purine metabolism; apoptosis; and fatty acid degradation (Figure 3C). In contrast, DMs in leg muscles in CR4_LM vs. CR6_LM and CR4_LM vs. CR8_LM, were mainly enriched in ABC transporters; glycerophospholipid metabolism; nucleotide metabolism; and D-Amino acid metabolism (Figure 3D, E). In CR6_LM vs. CR8_LM, the DMs were mainly enriched in valine, leucine and isoleucine biosynthesis, and D-amino acid metabolism (Figure 3F). These results suggest distinct metabolic pathways influencing breast and leg muscle composition.

Temporal Expression Trend Analysis of Differential Metabolites. To comprehensively investigate the change trend of metabolites in the muscles during the development of Lueyang black-bone chicken, the temporal expression patterns of DMs were analyzed (Figure S2).
Temporal expression trend analysis of DMs in breast muscles (A and B) and leg muscles (C and D) of Lueyang black-bone chickens at different ages.
Figure 4

Trend analysis identified 8 metabolic clusters in breast muscles, with clusters 0, 1, and 6 exhibiting significant age-dependent changes (Figure 4A). The three clusters contained 30, 26, and 13 DMs, respectively (Figure 4B). The heat map analysis illustrated that peptides and amino acid derivatives such as Thr-Pro-Asp and leucylleucine, accumulated in CR4, while 3-hydroxyeicosanylcarnitine, NADH increases in CR6 and CR8.

In the leg muscles, 8 trends were identified, with clusters 0, 1, and 7 demonstrating significant age-dependent changes (Figure 4C), comprising 18, 27, and 15 DMs, respectively. In particularly, peptides and amino acids accumulated in CR4, while PC and LysoPC showed increased accumulation in CR8 (Figure 4D). The metabolic shifts between CR6 and CR8 were less pronounced compared to those between CR4 and CR6, suggesting a slowing of metabolic changes beyond six months of age.
Analysis of Volatile Organic Compounds in Chicken Meat

A total of 48 and 47 VOCs were identified in BM and LM, respectively. Aldehydes, ketones, and alcohols were the dominant compounds contributing to meat flavor in both breast and leg muscles of Lueyang black-bone chickens.

Analysis of volatile substances in the breast muscles (A) and leg muscles (B) of Lueyang black-bone chickens of different ages. The dots in the fingerprint represent volatile compounds. Black is the background, while low content is indicated by light blue, high content by yellow, and higher content by red.
Figure 5

In breast muscles, CR4 exhibited relatively low levels of aldehydes, ketones, and alcohols, with key compounds including 3-methylbutyraldehyde, butanal, and benzaldehyde. CR6 showed an increase in ketones (e.g., 2-heptanone and acetoin) and alcohols (e.g., 1-penten-3-ol and 1-octen-3-ol). CR8 demonstrated the highest VOC content, with a notable increase in aldehydes (e.g., 1-octanal, 1-hexanal), ketones (e.g., 4-methyl-2-pentanone), alcohols (e.g., 3-octanol), and the presence of furan compounds such as 2-pentyl furan, indicating enhanced flavor development (Figure 5A).

In leg muscles, CR4 contained lower VOC levels, mainly dominated by aldehydes (e.g., 3-methylbutyraldehyde, heptanal) and ketones (e.g., acetone, cyclohexanone). CR6 had a distinct but minimal increase in 1-penten-3-ol. In contrast, CR8 exhibited the most diverse VOC profile, including significant increases in aldehydes (e.g., benzaldehyde, 1-hexanal), ketones (e.g., 2-heptanone), alcohols (e.g., 3-octanol, 2-methyl-2-propanol), esters (e.g., ethyl acetate), and acids (e.g., acetic acid), reinforcing the role of age in flavor compound formation (Figure 5B).
Correlation Analysis of Differential Metabolites with Volatile Organic Compounds
Correlation analysis of differential metabolites with volatile substances in breast muscles (A) and leg muscles(B).
Figure 6

A total of 71 differential metabolites were selected from the breast muscles in different ages. Among them, the concentrations of 3-hydroxyeicosanoylcarnitine, tetradecanoylcarnitine, 5-hydroxyhexadecanoylcarnitine, and decanoylcarnitine were significantly higher in CR8-BM. These carnitines exhibited positive correlations with aldehydes (pentanal dimer, 1-octanal, 1-hexanal dimer), alcohols (2-methyl-2-propanol, 2-butanol, 2-propanol), and ketone (4-methyl-2-pentanone monomer) (Figure 6A). Conversely, metabolites such as docosanedioate, trehalose, and genipin were predominantly accumulated in CR4-BM. These compounds showed positive correlations with 2-butanone, 3-methylbutanal monomer, and cyclohexanone, while exhibiting negative correlations with 1-octen-3-ol, 1-hexanal, and 1-pentanol.

A total of 74 differential metabolites were selected from the leg muscles in different ages. A variety of amino acids and peptides (Ile-Pro-Gln, n-stearoyl arginine, valyltyrosine, etc.), along with n-cyclopropanecarboxamide and phaseolic acid, were enriched in CR4-LM. These metabolites displayed significant positive correlations with aldehydes (1-octanal, nonanal, pentanal dimer), ketones (acetone, cyclohexanone, 2-butanone dimer), and alcohol (2-propanol) (Figure 6B). In contrast, phospholipids (PC(P-16:0/0:0), PI (18:1 (9Z)/0:0)), (2E,4E)-2,4-dodecadienal, and n-acetyl-L-glutamic acid were highly accumulated in CR8-LM, showing positive correlations with alcohols (3-octanol, ethanol) and ketones (2-heptanone monomer). These findings indicate that as chickens age, metabolic shifts influence VOC composition, with CR8 exhibiting a higher abundance of lipid-derived metabolites, which contribute to meat flavor development.
Discussion

With the increasing demand for high-quality poultry products, understanding the influence of slaughter age on meat quality has become essential for optimizing consumer preferences and production efficiency. Lueyang black-bone chickens are valued for their rich nutritional profile, including amino acids, unsaturated fatty acids, and bioactive compounds. However, variations in meat quality and flavor development at different slaughter ages necessitate a comprehensive investigation to provide scientific guidance for producers and consumers.

This study highlights a significant correlation between slaughter age and carcass yield. The observed weight increments:0.29 kg from 4-month-old (CR4) to 6-month-old (CR6) chickens and 0.14 kg from CR6 to 8-month-old (CR8):indicate a decelerating growth pattern, consistent with findings in other slow-growing breeds such as Da-Heng chickens and geese. This suggests that carcass development plateaus after six months, making it a critical age for economic considerations in poultry farming. The increase in shear force with age, likely due to muscle fiber hypertrophy, aligns with prior studies on poultry texture changes, reinforcing the trade-off between tenderness and meat yield.

Metabolite analysis revealed distinct biochemical shifts across slaughter ages. Amino acids, peptides, and phospholipids were predominant in younger chickens, particularly in CR4 breast muscles. These molecules contribute to meat flavor by enhancing umami and sweetness, in agreement with previous studies that link specific amino acids such as Asp and Glu to umami perception. Most of the peptides, such as Thr-Pro-Asp, Pro-Tyr-leu, Ile-Glu-Leu-Lys were accumulated in breast muscles and Asp-Ile-Glu, Leu-Pro-Thr, Pro-Glu-Ala were accumulated in leg muscles in CR4. These peptides may enhance flavor to the chicken meat. Additionally, the presence of phosphatidylinositol (PI) and phosphatidylserine (PS) in higher amounts in CR4 breast muscles suggests a role in maintaining membrane integrity and influencing flavor precursor formation. Conversely, carnitine derivatives, such as 3-hydroxyeicosanoylcarnitine, were significantly enriched in CR8 breast muscles, indicating a shift towards lipid metabolism and beta-oxidation, a phenomenon also observed in other slow-growing chicken breeds. These metabolic changes suggest that younger chickens rely more on amino acid metabolism, while older chickens exhibit enhanced lipid oxidation, a key factor in meat flavor development.

Volatile organic compounds, which are crucial determinants of meat aroma, also varied significantly with age. The volatile organic compounds in meat are mainly concentrated in aldehydes, alcohols, ketone, esters, acids and other categories. Aldehydes, including hexanal, heptanal, and nonanal, were more abundant in CR8 breast muscles, consistent with increased lipid oxidation at older ages. It has been indicated that many aldehydes have a pleasant aroma, such as pentanal has a "woody, fruity aroma", hexanal has a "green, grasslike" aroma and heptanal has a "fruity, fatty aroma". The presence of 1-octen-3-ol, a key alcohol derived from lipid hydroperoxide degradation, was higher in CR6 and CR8, reinforcing the role of lipid oxidation in poultry meat flavor. These findings corroborate reports on Chinese native chicken breeds, where aldehydes and alcohols are primary contributors to flavor complexity. Additionally, CR4 leg muscles exhibited a relatively high concentration of amino acid-derived aldehydes and ketones, suggesting that amino acid metabolism plays a more prominent role in younger chickens, while lipid oxidation dominates in older birds.

The relationship between metabolites and volatile organic compounds further illustrates age-related differences in flavor formation. Amino acids, lipids, and nucleotides serve as primary precursors for VOCs, with their transformation occurring through Maillard reactions, Strecker degradation, and lipid oxidation. The accumulation of carnitine derivatives, such as 11-methylnonadecanoylcarnitine and decanoylcarnitine, in CR8 breast muscles suggests enhanced fatty acid beta-oxidation, which may contribute to the generation of VOCs such as 2-propanol, pentanal dimer, and 1-octanal. Similarly, phospholipid hydrolysis:facilitated by phospholipases A1 and A2:plays a critical role in VOC formation. The higher levels of phospholipids, including PG (22:6), PC (P-16:0), and PI (18:1), in CR8 leg muscles suggest their potential involvement in producing alcohols and aldehydes, such as 1-octen-3-ol and ethanol.

Moreover, amino acid metabolism was particularly active in CR4 leg muscles, where peptides (Ile-Pro-Gln, Leu-Pro-Thr, Pro-Le-Ser) and amino acid derivatives (n-stearoyl arginine, valyltyrosine) were significantly enriched. These metabolites may promote the formation of aldehydes (1-octanal, n-nonanal, methylbutanal monomer) and ketones (2-butanone, acetone, cyclohexanone), which contribute to the characteristic flavor of younger chickens. In contrast, lipid-derived VOCs, particularly aldehydes and alcohols, were more abundant in older chickens, supporting the notion that lipid oxidation becomes the dominant contributor to flavor development with age.
Conclusion

This study provides new insights into how slaughter age influences meat quality, metabolite composition, and flavor characteristics in Lueyang black-bone chickens. Younger chickens (CR4) exhibit superior tenderness and amino acid-derived flavor compounds, while older chickens (CR8) develop richer lipid-derived VOCs, contributing to a more pronounced aroma profile. Additionally, the minimal metabolic differences between CR6 and CR8 suggest that the most significant biochemical changes occur before six months of age. Future studies should further explore the molecular pathways governing these metabolic transitions to enhance meat quality in slow-growing poultry breeds.

passages.text: Harnessing machine learning to predict and prevent proximal junctional kyphosis and failure in adult spinal deformity surgery: A systematic review
Introduction

Adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery involves high costs and risks, with Proximal Junctional Kyphosis (PJK) and Proximal Junctional Failure (PJF) being major concerns. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer potential in predicting and preventing these complications. This review examines the role of AI in predicting PJK/PJF, its effectiveness, and future research needs.
Research question
Can AI-based models accurately predict PJK/PJF after ASD surgery, and what factors affect their performance?
Material and methods

A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, analyzing Medline, Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases up to December 2024. Keywords included "Adult Spinal Deformity," "PJK," "PJF," "AI," and "ML." Data extracted included study characteristics, patient demographics, surgical details, AI model parameters, and performance metrics. Bias risk was assessed using the MINORS score.
Results

Among 164 studies, 7 met inclusion criteria (n = 2179 patients). Mean age was 63.2 +- 3.7 years, BMI 26.1 +- 2.4 kg/m2, and fusion levels 9.82 +- 1.8. PJK/PJF occurred in 41.1 %. AI models (Random Forest, supervised learning) had accuracy from 72.5 % to 100 % (AUC up to 1.0). Key predictors included age, BMD, spinal alignment, and implant type.
Discussion and conclusions

AI and ML models show promise in predicting PJK/PJF after ASD surgery. However, larger multicenter studies with standardized definitions, BMD assessments, and preoperative MRI integration are needed for broader clinical application and validation.
Highlights
Machine learning enhances early risk identification for PJK after adult spinal deformity surgery.
RCTs should validate ML predictions by integrating standardized PJK/PJF definitions, preoperative MRI, and key radiographic parameter.
Accurate BMD assessment, UIV selection, and prophylactic measures are crucial for improving predictive models.
Introduction

Adult spinal deformity (ASD) refers to a diverse group of medical disorders characterized by alterations in the coronal and axial profiles, which typically arise in older adulthood. As the general population ages, the prevalence of ASD is expected to increase, with over 60 million older adults in the United States projected to have some form of spinal deformity by 2050. The development of ASD is typically associated with the onset of various types of pain symptoms, such as back pain, radiculopathy, and postural instability, which result in a significant reduction in quality of life. Compared to conservative treatment, surgical intervention improves patient-reported outcomes but also incurs significant healthcare-related financial costs. Moreover, the high risk of medical and mechanical complications during the perioperative period and in the long term further complicates the therapeutic decision-making process.

Among the most common mechanical complications of surgical treatment for ASD are those referred to under the umbrella term of proximal adjacent segment pathology (ASP), including Proximal Junctional Kyphosis (PJK) and Proximal Junctional Failure (PJF). Although its definition remains inconsistent, PJK is generally characterized by a progressive increase in the Proximal Junctional Angle (PJA) between the uppermost instrumented vertebra (UIV) and the vertebra two levels above (UIV + 2), with an incidence ranging from 20 % to 40 % of patients. If left untreated, PJK may advance to symptomatic PJF, which may require revision surgery in cases of impaired structural integrity or neurological deficits.

Over the years, numerous efforts have been made to identify risk factors and develop preventive strategies for complications by creating models that combine demographic, radiographic, and surgical data and advanced analytical techniques, such as regressions. Despite these advancements, a definitive consensus on accurately predicting ASP development remains elusive, as the complexity of its pathophysiology and numerous variables pose significant challenges in creating a universally reliable predictive framework, mainly because methods often rely on averages without accounting for individual variations or generate odds/hazard ratios for each variable.

In recent years, the progressive integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine has revolutionized the approach to diagnosis and therapeutic decision-making, thanks to its ability to analyze and learn from large amounts of data. In the field of spinal surgery, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models have brought tangible benefits, particularly in screening, spinal parameter calculation, and predicting the development of complications, especially after surgical interventions.

The potential role of AI in predicting the development of ASP could be relevant, enabling more accurate identification of patients at higher risk for developing PJK and PJF, thus enhancing clinical decision-making and precision medicine.

This article aims to review the existing literature on the role of AI in predicting and preventing PJK and PJF following surgery for ASD, while also discussing the advantages, limitations, and prospects for improving the management of these complex conditions.
Materials and methods
Study selection and eligibility criteria

AI: Artificial Intelligence; ASD: Adult Spinal Deformity; AUC: Area Under the Curve; AUPRC: Area Under The Precision-Recall Curve; AUROC: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristics; PJK: Proximal Junctional Kyphosis; PJF: Proximal Junctional Failure; RCT: Randomized-Controlled Trials; 3-D: 3-Dimensional.

A systematic review was performed to explore research on the application of AI-based predictive models for forecasting the development of PJK/PJF after surgical treatment for ASD, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The inclusion and exclusion criteria were established before the commencement of the study (Table 1). The formulation of the research question was done using a PIOS approach: Population (P), Intervention (I), Outcome (O), and Study Design (S). This systematic review collected and analyzed data on patients who underwent ASD surgery (P). ML-based predictive models (I) were adopted to evaluate accuracy and/or Area Under the Curve (AUC)/Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristics (AUROC)/Area Under The Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) in the prediction of PJK/PJF (O). The following study designs were included (S): Randomized Control Trials (RCT), Retrospective Cohort studies (RC), Prospective Cohort studies (PC), and comparative studies.
Search strategy

A thorough search of electronic databases, including Medline, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, was performed from the inception of each database to December 2024. The search was filtered for "humans" and "English" language articles. The following search string was used: ((Adult Spinal Deformity) OR (Scoliosis) OR (Spinal Curvature)) AND ((Proximal Junctional Kyphosis) OR (PJK) OR (Proximal Junctional Failure) OR (PJF) OR (Proximal Junctional Angle) OR (PJA)) AND ((Artificial Intelligence) OR (Deep Learning) OR (Machine Learning) OR (Predictive Model)).
Data collection process
PRISMA Flow Diagram demonstrating the number of included studies.
Fig. 1

Two independent reviewers (P.B. and S.D.S.) screened each article in two stages. Initially, article titles and abstracts were screened, followed by a full-text review of the selected articles. Any disagreements were resolved by consulting with the senior author (L.O.). The inclusion and exclusion of the reviewed articles are reported below in the PRISMA flowchart, found in Fig. 1.
Data items

The extracted data from each article included the first author, publication year, study type, Level of Evidence (LOE), country, journal, study objectives, inclusion and exclusion criteria, methods for radiographic parameter calculation, AI model type, training/testing ratio, definitions of PJK/PJF, and PJA measurement. Patient demographics and follow-up details, such as total patient count, case/control numbers, age, sex, and Body Mass Index (BMI), were collected. Intervention-related data, including primary or revision surgery, preoperative-Scoliosis Research Society (SRS)-Schwab coronal curve type and global balance (GB) modifier, UIV and lower instrumented vertebra (LIV) levels, number of fused segments, number of 3-Column Osteotomies (3-CO), and implant type, were also recorded. Furthermore, ML algorithm performance metrics:accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, AUC, AUROC, and AUPRC:were analyzed.

The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS), which evaluates the quality of comparative studies (Table 2). No RCTs were found. The MINORS tool consists of 12 items: clear study aim, inclusion of consecutive patients, prospective data collection, endpoints appropriate to the study's goal, unbiased assessment of endpoints, suitable follow-up duration, less than 5 % follow-up loss, prospective calculation of sample size, an adequate control group, contemporary comparison groups, baseline group equivalence, and proper statistical analysis. Each reviewer rated these items individually. The scoring system assigns 0 for no report, 1 for inadequate reporting, and 2 for adequate reporting, with a maximum possible global score of 20 for Non-randomized controlled trials (NRCTs). Due to its simplicity, MINORS is easily applicable to readers and researchers, and its reliability has been documented. Using this tool, the potential risk of bias in the selected studies was independently evaluated by two authors (P.B. and S.D.S). In cases where the reviewers disagreed, a third independent reviewer (L.O.) made the final decision.
Results
Study selection

The initial database search identified 164 records. After removing duplicates, 69 unique records remained. Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, resulting in the exclusion of 51 records. The full texts of the remaining 18 articles were assessed for eligibility. A total of 7 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the study. The PRISMA flow diagram details the study selection process (Fig. 1).
Study characteristics

No RCTs met the inclusion criteria. All included studies were RC, either multicenter or single-center, and qualified as LOE four or higher. Seven NRCTs were identified, published between 2016 and 2023: six had a LOE of 3, and one had a LOE of 4. A total of 2179 patients were used to train, validate, and test the AI models. The studies showed acceptable homogeneity in terms of objectives, ASD definition, and inclusion and exclusion criteria. ASD was defined as a pathologic condition in patients aged> 18 years old presenting with a scoliosis coronal Cobb angle >=20 , Sagittal Vertical Axis (SVA) >= 5 cm, Pelvic Tilt (PT) >= 25 , and/or Thoracic Kyphosis (TK) >=60 . The minimum follow-up required was one year in the studies by Lee et al. and Lafage et al., while the others required at least two years of follow-up imaging. Study characteristics are summarized in Table 2.

The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS). On the whole, the studies exhibited a moderate risk of bias, with an average MINORS score of 16.5, indicating several methodological limitations. Notable strengths included clearly defined objectives, appropriate endpoints for the study aims, and the inclusion of consecutive patients in all studies. However, common weaknesses included the absence of prospective data collection and the lack of prospective sample size calculations, which were key factors in the heightened risk of bias. While these studies provide useful insights, the moderate risk of bias calls for careful interpretation of the results. Future research should address these methodological flaws to enhance the quality of evidence in this area. A detailed breakdown of the MINORS scores for each study can be found in Table 3.

Table 4, Table 5 summarize the type of predictive AI, the data used for training, validation, and testing, as well as the definitions of PJK and PJF applied in the studies. A diverse range of  models were employed, including C5.0 algorithms for decision tree building, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Support Vector Machine models (SVMs). The training/testing ratio of 70:30 was consistent across the studies, with Lafage et al. and Johnson et al. further dividing the testing samples into validation and testing subsets, to prevent overfitting. The studies showed mild heterogeneity in demographic, surgical, and radiographic variables. Demographically, the most commonly reported characteristics were age, sex, BMI, and prior fusion surgery. In terms of radiographic variables, several coronal and sagittal parameters were used for model training, including coronal parameters such as Cobb angles and sagittal parameters like SVA, TK, Lumbar Lordosis (LL), PT, Pelvic Incidence (PI) minus LL mismatch (PI-LL), T1 Pelvic Angle (TPA), and the SRS-Schwab adult spinal deformity classification. When reported, PJA was calculated as the sagittal Cobb angle between the lower end plate of the UIV and the upper end plate of the UIV+2. Definitions of PJK varied among studies. Some defined PJK as an increase in postoperative PJA >20  compared to baseline alone, or in addition to a deterioration of at least one SRS-Schwab sagittal modifier, while others defined it as an increase of >=10  alone, or with an increase of at least 10  from the preoperative measurement. PJF definitions also varied, with most studies defining it as an increase in PJA of at least 15  that may require revision surgery. Yagi et al. defined PJF as an increase of >=20  in PJA, along with deterioration of at least one SRS-Schwab sub-category grade compared to baseline immediately postoperative, or as any type of PJK requiring revision surgery.

Table 6, Table 7 summarize the demographic, surgical, radiographical, and outcome characteristics of the included studies. The studies included a mean of 311 +- 241 patients, with an average of 204 females (65.5 %). All studies provided baseline and final follow-up images, with some also including follow-up images at 6 weeks and 2 or 3 months. The average age of patients was 63.2 +- 3.7 years, the mean BMI was 26.1 +- 2.4 kg/m2, and the average number of levels fused per procedure was 9.82 +- 1.8. Of the included patients, 58.4 % underwent primary surgery, while 41.6 % had revision surgery. A total of 4 studies reported the preoperative SRS-Schwab Coronal Curve Type, while 3 studies reported the preoperative SRS-Schwab GB modifier.

A total of 896 patients developed either PJK or PJF at the last follow-up (41.1 %). Scheer et al. found that the PJK/PJF group had significantly higher mean baseline PT, PI-LL, and SVA than the None group. Yagi et al. identified LIV at the pelvis, Schwab-SRS type N or L, severe PT, low UIV, and high baseline PI-LL mismatch as significant risk factors for PJF. Tretiakov et al. concluded that patients with greater PT and TPA offsets, those more likely to be under-corrected according to Sagittal Age-adjusted Score (SAAS) scoring, and those with a UIV of T10 or lower or LIV at the sacrum, were more prone to PJK or PJF in the postoperative period. Lee et al. found that after deformity correction, 42 % of patients achieved the ideal age-adjusted PI-LL, 44.5 % were under-corrected, and 13.4 % were overcorrected.

Table 8 presents a summary of the results of the ML models, along with their characteristics, including sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, recall, AUC/AUROC, and AUPRC, as well as the findings and conclusions of the included studies.
Assessment of key predictors of PJK/PJF Occurrence

Scheer et al.'s C5.0 algorithm decision tree predicted the onset of PJK/PJF with an overall accuracy of 86.3 % and an AUC of 0.89. The seven most significant predictors identified were age, LIV, preoperative SVA, UIV implant type, UIV, preoperative PT, and preoperative PI-LL. Yagi et al. trained two separate decision-making trees using the Tobuilda and C5.0 algorithms, one incorporating Bone Mineral Density (BMD) values and one without, finding that the inclusion of BMD significantly enhanced prediction accuracy, achieving an AUC of 1.0 when BMD was included. The nine most significant predictors for PJK were PT, BMD, LIV level (pelvis), UIV level, pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) application, global alignment (C7-SVA), BMI, PI-LL, and age. Tretiakov et al. achieved an AUC of 0.923 using a backstep conditional binary Supervised Learning (SL) model, identifying six key predictors of PJK/PJF: age >=74, high baseline SAAS TPA modifier, high PT modifier, fusion of >10 levels, no prophylaxis use, and a 6-week SAAS PI-LL modifier >1. In conclusion, Lee et al. used five different ML-models and found that the Random Forest (RF) model had the highest accuracy (83 %) and AUROC (0.76).
Preventive measures for PJK development

Tretiakov et al. found that prophylactic measures like cementing, hooks, tethers, and hybrid methods could help prevent PJK and PJF, with the SAAS scoring system being a strong predictor of junctional degeneration. Yagi et al. emphasized the importance of BMD in predicting PJK/PJF and recommended low BMD as a key factor, advising teriparatide treatment and UIV+1 tethering as preventive strategies.
Soft tissue characteristics' impact in PJK

Johnson et al. developed three distinct machine learning models to predict PJK following ASD surgery. Their final model (Model 3), which utilized raw thoracic T1 magnetic resonance images (MRIs), achieved higher sensitivity (73.1 %) and specificity (79.5 %) compared to earlier models. The study concluded that soft tissue features were the primary factors in all accurate positive radiographic PJK predictions.
Replication of surgeon decision-making in UIV selection

Lafage et al.'s analysis focused on developing an ANN to replicate surgeon decision-making in UIV selection, using preoperative data and alignment objectives, and to assess the risk of PJK postoperatively. Their results showed an accuracy of 81 %, precision and recall of 87.5 %, and an overall AUC of 0.829, revealing a larger residual coronal Cobb angle and greater TK in the Upper Thoracic (UT) group, though there were no significant differences in PJK rates.
Identification of major risk factors for Unplanned Reoperations (UROs)

Ryu et al. developed four distinct ML models to identify the key risk factors, including PJK and PJF, for UROs following corrective surgery for ASD. Their analysis found that the RF model demonstrated the highest accuracy (72.5 %) and AUROC/AUPRC (0.73/0.82), with postoperative SVA, PJF, and their interactions identified as key risk factors for UROs following ASD surgery.
Discussion

This systematic review analyzed data from 2179 patients across seven studies evaluating AI models for predicting and preventing PJK/PJF following ASD surgery. The findings highlight the potential of ML algorithms in managing these complex cases, demonstrating that various models can be effectively and flexibly utilized to predict ASP development in many surgically treated ASD patients.
Strengths, limitations, and applications of AI predictive models in ASD surgery

Over the past decade, AI has revolutionized medicine by improving diagnostic imaging, disease prediction, and patient management, leading to better clinical outcomes. Notably, ML models have shown promise in predicting postoperative outcomes and reducing complications, offering improved accuracy by identifying data relationships and minimizing bias compared to traditional methods. The training of these models involves testing with common splits of 80:20 or 70:30 and iterative cross-validation on separate datasets to optimize predictive performance. As a result, ML models offer significantly more powerful predictive capabilities than statistical models, but their complexity often makes them more challenging to interpret. Indeed, its integration presents challenges such as automation bias, ethical concerns regarding data privacy, algorithm transparency, and decision-making biases, which require careful attention. To maximize AI's benefits while minimizing risks, rigorous validation, regulatory oversight, and collaboration with clinical expertise are necessary.

AI models have become increasingly prevalent in spinal surgery, assisting clinicians in early imaging assessment, automated analysis of radiographic parameters, treatment planning, and prognostic predictions. Hence, AI-driven algorithms have been developed to enhance surgical planning and optimize patient-specific strategies in ASD, a complex condition that requires meticulous treatment planning and could greatly benefit from ML predictive models. A range of predictive tools have already been employed in ASD management, extending from forecasting the length of hospital stay and the need for blood transfusions to predicting perioperative or postoperative complications such as pseudoarthrosis, malalignments and ASP.
Key predictors and preventive measures for PJK/PJF occurrence

Over the years, numerous radiographical classification methods have been applied to predict and prevent ASP. Indeed, radiological parameters may play a key role in assessing the risk of complications following ASD surgery, with tools such as the SRS-Schwab Classification, Age Adjusted Sagittal Alignment, GAP score, and Roussouly Classification being commonly used. However, no single system can reliably predict such complications, suggesting the need to adopt of a holistic approach that combines various patient-specific factors and predictive models to achieve optimal outcomes. Therefore, preoperative planning must include careful considerations, such as assessing the patient's BMD and modifying the surgical technique. These adjustments may involve avoiding overcorrection, limiting fusion levels, employing cement-augmented pedicle screws at the UIV and UIV+1, adding ligament augmentation at the UIV levels, and contouring the terminal rod. Two studies in this review explored the impact of prophylactic surgical techniques on PJK/PJF, with Tretiakov et al. suggesting cementing and tethers as preventive measures and Yagi et al. highlighting low BMD as a key factor, recommending teriparatide and UIV+1 tethering for prevention.
The impact of soft tissue characteristics on PJK

ML models are trained using MRI images in various medical fields. In spinal surgery, these images are frequently used to assess lumbar intervertebral disc degeneration, muscle composition, and their role in disease progression. For example, Tian et al. developed an MRI-based predictive model for PJK/PJF, combining bone and paraspinal muscle quality metrics, and found that paraspinal muscle and vertebral bone quality are more influential than radiographic alignment in predicting PJK/PJF in ASD correction patients. In the included study by Johnson et al., two predictive algorithms were developed: the first (Model 1) using only demographic, radiographic variables, and intended fusion levels, and the second (Model 2) incorporating raw scoliosis images. A third model (Model 3) was then created by adding preoperative thoracic T1 MRI images to the variables from Model 1. This model demonstrated a significant increase in sensitivity and specificity in predicting radiographic PJK risk, concluding that soft tissue information and its degeneration at the T1 level may play a crucial role in forecasting postoperative ASP.
The influence of UIV selection on the development of PJK

The selection of the UIV in ASD correction is considered a crucial aspect. UIV in the UT spine may provide more stable correction and lower rates of PJK and PJF, while a UIV in the LT spine may offer benefits such as reduced operative time, blood loss, costs, and risk of soft tissue failure, especially in high-BMI patients. Kumar et al. recently proposed an algorithm for selecting the UIV in long-segment fusions, concluding that the choice should be made after considering various patient characteristics, including preoperative alignment, comorbidities, as well as surgeon-specific and facility-specific factors. Nevertheless, a consensus on the selection of the UIV in ASD surgery has yet to be reached. The study by Lafage et al. in this review aimed to create an algorithm that replicates the decision-making process of experienced surgeons in selecting the UIV, incorporating demographic data, preoperative coronal and sagittal alignment, postoperative pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch, and postoperative alignment goals. They found that, at one year, the revision rate was 11.9 %, and the rate of radiographic PJK was 29.4 %, with no significant difference between the UT and LT groups. Thus, predictive algorithms offer considerable potential in assisting with the accurate selection of the UIV, thereby opening the door for future research focused on validating these algorithms for UIV prediction and PJK/PJF prevention in the treatment of ASD.
Selecting the correct AI predictive model

The selection of the appropriate AI model and the rationale behind its use remains an ongoing subject of debate. Lee et al. and Ryu et al. demonstrated that models like RF can achieve the highest accuracy and AUC in predicting the development of PJK and identifying key factors influencing UROs. However, Tretiakov et al. employed a SL predictive analysis to improve the transparency of the factors being studied, emphasizing that RF models, while powerful, can lead to an overestimation of target outcomes due to increased out-of-bag error in binary classification tasks. This highlights the importance of carefully considering model limitations and the specific context in which they are applied. For this reason, further comprehensive studies are required to validate the superiority of one model over another.
Limitations

The present review has several limitations that must be acknowledged. Due to their absence in the literature, no RCTs or prospective studies were included. Additionally, there is a significant lack of consistency in the predictive algorithms, training variables, definitions of PJK/PJF, and intervention outcomes across the included studies. In conclusion, the algorithms were trained on a relatively small number of patients, with some studies including as few as 143 patients, which limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions on the subject.

For these reasons, there is an urgent need for prospective multicenter RCTs with larger sample sizes that incorporate the parameters outlined in the following study, mainly including a precise assessment of patients' BMD values, utilizing all radiographic variables (SRS-Schwab Classification, Age Adjusted Sagittal Alignment, GAP score, Roussouly Classification, and SAAS scoring system), employing a standardized definition of PJK/PJF, thoroughly assessing the impact of prophylactic measures and UIV selection, and integrating the algorithm with preoperative MRI images are essential steps to further validate the findings of this review.

Nevertheless, the current review highlights that studies utilizing ML predictive algorithms for evaluating postoperative PJK/PJF in ASD patients show potential, offering valuable insights into improving outcomes and enhancing surgical planning and patient management.
Conclusion

The ability to predict and prevent the development of ASP with certainty in the complex surgical context of ASD patients could represent a pivotal breakthrough. The present analysis provides convincing evidence of the considerable potential of ML algorithms in the prediction and prevention of PJK/PJF. Future research should focus on prospective multicenter RCTs with larger sample sizes, employing a standardized definition of PJK/PJF, careful evaluation of prophylactic measures and UIV selection, accurate assessments of patients' BMD values, a comprehensive range of radiographic variables and scoring systems, and the integration of preoperative MRI images, to further validate the findings of this review.

passages.text: Strengthening Antimicrobial Stewardship in Korea: Strategies to Address Workforce Gaps and Expand ASP Nationwide

Given the global threat of antimicrobial-resistant organisms, an effective antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP) is essential. Infectious disease (ID) physicians and ID-trained pharmacists are prioritized as critical core members of ASP in hospital settings, but securing these ID-trained professionals in all settings is challenging. Alternative champions and personnel for implementation may be needed. This narrative review highlights the efficacy of ASP when non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists are engaged in ASP, showcasing various studies demonstrating significant improvements in antimicrobial utilization, cost, and patient outcomes. Additionally, it discusses the impact of network-based models, such as the Duke Antimicrobial Stewardship Outreach Network, which provides structured support and resources to lower-resourced hospitals to ensure the successful implementation of ASP. Ultimately, this narrative review provides insights into how to structure accountability and pharmacy/stewardship expertise in establishing and expanding ASP nationwide in Korea, where ASP is still in its early stages. In addressing this issue, government initiatives to actively support this effort are essential, and striving to develop evidence-based policies is necessary.
Introduction

Antimicrobial stewardship (AS) refers to coordinated interventions designed to improve and measure the appropriate use of antimicrobial agents by promoting the selection of the optimal antimicrobial drug regimen, including dosing, duration of therapy, and route of administration. Various interventions and strategies can be utilized to achieve goals of AS, including audit and feedback, antimicrobial restriction and authorization of prescription for specific antimicrobials, guideline development, and education.

While these interventions often require financial support for hiring personnel and establishing systems, AS can lead to multiple types of benefits. First, AS has been proposed as an important approach to overcome the global antimicrobial resistance crisis. Second, AS can reduce costs associated with antimicrobial use (AU), length of stay (LOS), and diagnosis. Third, AS can protect patients from the side effects of antimicrobial agents. Ultimately, AS is expected to improve patient's outcomes such as LOS, readmission rate, and mortality rate. Therefore, investing in AS in hospitals yields benefits not only from a national public health perspective, but also by improving the operational efficacy of hospitals and enhancing the quality of patient care.

Two core elements of the hospital AS program (ASP) are accountability, which involves appointing a leader or co-leaders responsible for ASP management and outcomes, and pharmacy/stewardship expertise, which involves appointing a pharmacist with specific training to lead implementation efforts. An Infectious diseases (ID) physician is a physician who specializes in ID after completing a fellowship training in ID and getting board certification. An ID-trained pharmacist usually means a pharmacist who completed a post-graduate year (PGY) 1 residency followed by a PGY2 residency in ID. A Board-Certified Infectious Diseases Pharmacistis a pharmacist who fulfills all the eligible requirements and gets certification from the Board of Pharmacy Specialties Speciality Councils in the United States (US). These are ideal personnel for both of these roles. However, it remains challenging to find these specialized personnel in many healthcare settings. Thus, from a national perspective, the participation of non-ID trained physicians and/or pharmacists in ASP is essential. ID physicians and/or ID-trained pharmacists-guided network-based models can facilitate the involvement of non-ID-trained physicians and/or pharmacists in ASP. This issue is particularly important in Korea where, to date, resources to support the development of ASP have been insufficient. This narrative review explores the role of non-ID-trained physicians and/or pharmacists and network-based models in ASP and aims to provide perspective on accountability and pharmacy/stewardship expertise as core elements of ASP in Korea.
The importance of ID physicians and ID pharmacists in ASP

ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists are the most qualified personnel to fulfill the core element of pharmacy/stewardship expertise. Several studies have demonstrated that hospital ASP can be highly effective by engaging these experts. One retrospective study involved the review of 290 patients receiving inpatient parenteral antibiotics at two US Veterans Affairs medical centers. Cases were reviewed for compliance with indicators of appropriate antimicrobial stewardship. Several indicators were higher at the hospital with a dedicated ID-trained AS pharmacist compared to the hospital that assigned AS duties to ward pharmacists, including initial antimicrobial therapy that adhered to local treatment guidelines (96.8% vs. 87%; P <0.002), modification of therapy within 24 hours of availability of laboratory data (86.7% vs. 72.6%; P <0.03), and discontinuation of antibiotics when a patient's illness was not caused by bacterial infection (78.0% vs. 33.3%; P <0.002) . Similarly, a cluster randomized controlled trial performed in 15 hospitals in Utah, compared antimicrobial utilization metrics between hospitals with active AS interventions (receiving antibiotic audit and feedback on the majority of antibiotics, antibiotic restriction through an ID physician or ID-trained pharmacist, and regularly review of microbiology results) and those with passive AS interventions (basic AS education and tools, access to an ID hotline, AU data, audit and feedback for select antibiotics, and locally controlled antibiotic restrictions). Hospitals receiving active interventions had reductions in total (rate ratio [RR], 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.80-0.99) and broad-spectrum (RR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.63-0.91) AU. In comparison, there was no reduction in hospitals receiving passive interventions. Next, In a recent study analyzing clinical scenario responses from 139 physicians (19 ID physicians, 62 hospitalists, and 58 other internists) in 16 Veterans' Affairs medical centers in the US, a higher proportion of ID physicians answered correctly in cellulitis scenario, compared to hospitalists and other internists (concordance: ID physicians, 76%; hospitalists, 58%; other internists, 52%; P=0.0087). In a study involving 423 patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia at 16 community hospitals in the US between 2009 and 2019, patients who received AS telehealth service, including ID physicians consultations and ID-trained pharmacists surveillance, demonstrated significantly higher bundle adherence rates (79% in case vs. 23% in control; P <0.01). In a retrospective single center study including 1,691 patients with candidemia from 2002 to 2015 in the US, ID consultation was significantly associated with lower 90-day mortality in the model with inverse weighting by the propensity score (hazard ratio, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.73-0.91]). Finally, a narrative review of the impact of ID physicians and/or ID-trained pharmacists on AS including 31 studies published from 1980 to 2013 showed that the presence of ID physicians and/or ID-trained pharmacists was associated with a significant improvement in the appropriateness of antibiotics in almost all studies.
Current status of ID physicians and ID-trained or certified pharmacists in Korea

In 2019, there were only 242 ID physicians in Korea, representing 0.42/100,000 of the population and the average number of beds per ID physician was 342 beds. As of 2022, there are 281 ID physicians and 71 ID pediatricians. Their median weekly working hours from Monday to Saturday was 60.5 hours (interquartile range, 53.5-71 hours). These clinicians handle a wide range of tasks, including high volumes and complex patient care, leadership positions in infection control, research, and clinical education. As of 2022, there are 45 tertiary general hospitals (47,021 beds), 326 general hospitals with more than 100 beds (107,683 beds), 1,398 hospitals with more than 30 beds (128,366 beds), and 1,435 nursing hospitals (271.785 beds) in Korea. According to a survey conducted in 2019, 51.6% of ID physicians are employed at tertiary hospitals, and 40.2% are working at general hospitals. Regionally, 38.6% of ID physicians work in Seoul, and the number of ID physicians per population is significantly lower in other regions. Except for Seoul, Busan, Daegu, Incheon, and Gyeongsangnam-do, the number of ID physicians is less than 10 in 12 broad local government areas. Overall, it is challenging for individual hospitals to secure ID physicians. Given their broad clinical responsibilities, it is also difficult for ID physicians to dedicate sufficient time to AS.

The Certified Pharmacy Specialties (CPS) by The Korean Society of Health-System Pharmacists was introduced in Korea in 2008, and the first CPS pharmacist was certified in Korea in 2010. The first ID CPS was certified in 2016, and there are 140 ID CPS pharmacists in 54 hospitals in Korea as of 2022. To be eligible for the CPS exam, one must complete over 200 hours of standard courses and more than 160 hours of specialized theoretical courses, including practice. The CPS certification is awarded to those who pass both the first and second rounds of the exam. The status of ID CPS by region and type of healthcare institution is shown in Table 1. Most ID CPS pharmacists work at tertiary general hospitals (77.9%). Starting in 2024, the Korean Minister of Health and Welfare began granting the certification for pharmacy specialties. To become an ID-trained pharmacist, one must complete a one-year or specified duration training program conducted by accredited training institutions.

In summary, securing ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists for ASP in Korea presents a significant challenge. These valuable professionals, equipped with pharmacy/stewardship expertise, are in short supply and already have too many hats, leaving them limited capacity to take on additional ASP duties. According to a 2018 nationwide survey, only a few hospitals in Korea have ASP teams staffed with full-time ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists. While securing ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists for ASP is extremely important, relying solely on these experts for ASP will limit nationwide expansion.
The role of non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists in ASP

The shortage of ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists is challenging in Korea and many countries, including the US. As a result, some ASP utilize strategies where non-ID-trained physicians and/or pharmacists lead ASP (Table 2). In a pre-and post-analysis done in a single center in Japan with ASP teams consisting of non-ID-trained physicians, pharmacists, nurses, microbiologists, and administrative staff, ASP was associated with appropriate empirical antifungal therapy (100% vs. 60.0%; proportion ratio, 1.67; 95% CI, 1.24-2.23), appropriate duration of treatment (84.7% vs. 43.3%; proportion ratio, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.28-3.00), removal of central venous catheters (94.4% vs. 70.8%; proportion ratio, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.02-1.74), and ophthalmological examination (93.5% vs. 63.3%; proportion ratio, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.12-1.96) in hospital-acquired candidemia. A multicentre, prospective cohort study of adult community-acquired pneumonia patients hospitalized between July 2017 and July 2018 in 39 hospitals across South Africa showed that implementation of the community-acquired pneumonia bundle that non-ID-trained pharmacists used to audit compliance and provide feedback was associated with improved compliance with AS process measures from 45.3% to 51.6% (P <0.0001). In a prospective study from Canada, in which the ASP was initially led by a dedicated ID-trained pharmacist and then transitioned to a ward-based pharmacist, the acceptance rate for AS recommendations was maintained above 82% despite the transition in leadership, although fewer patients were exposed to the AS intervention after the transition. In a hospital with hospitalist-led interdisciplinary AS interventions, an educational bundle with daily rounding with an internal medicine-trained clinical pharmacist reduced the total AU by 33%. In a prospective multicenter study in China, non-ID-trained pharmacists-led ID consultation could improve prognosis in the context of other controlled confounders (adjusted odds ratio, 1.838; 95% CI, 1.212-2.786). Overall, non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists can have significant roles in ASP through various modalities such as training, education, certification programs, providing protocol and guidelines, clinical decision support systems, and tele-stewardship or tele-consulting. However, concerns remain regarding publication bias, which may overestimate the effectiveness of ASP activities led by non-ID-trained physicians and/or pharmacists. Depending on the specific circumstances of each hospital, various scenarios can be considered for staffing the pharmacy expertise within ASP team.

The role of network-based models in ASP

The network-based model is an important strategy for overcoming the shortage of ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists and expanding ASP in various types of healthcare institutions, such as community hospitals, critical access hospitals, and long-term care facilities. Buckel et al. classified the healthcare network model into four main approaches: collaborative, centrally coordinated, centrally led, and collaborative, consultative network (Table 3). Centrally led approach is the most common network model in the US (40.0%), followed by centrally coordinated (30.0%), collaborative (15.0%), and the collaborative, consultative approach (10.0%).

Duke Antimicrobial Stewardship Outreach Network (DASON) is a representative collaborative, consultative ASP model in the US, in which nearly 40 community hospitals participate. Enrolled community hospitals in DASON receive multiple services, including data collection, analysis, feedback, educational resources, and expert consultation on ASP management and processes, but not on individual patients. Specific services include collecting AU and antimicrobial resistance data, creating network-wide benchmarks, providing on-site visits, monthly newsletters, and answers to frequently asked questions. A DASON liaison pharmacist with specialized training in ID and AS assists pharmacists, physicians, nurses, hospital leaders, microbiologists, information technologists and/or advanced practice practitioners in developing local stewardship activities. This exemplifies how pharmacy expertise is provided as a part of the DASON network model.

Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of networks for ASP (Table 4). For example, the Veterans Health Administrative (VHA) AS initiative and the VHA national AS taskforce provided services to U.S. VA medical centers through coordinated education (face-to-face conference, providing Sanford guideline, webinar, teleconference, and an internal VHA Antimicrobial Stewardship Microsoft SharePoint site), information gathering (survey), and policy development and dissemination starting in 2011. After these activities began, a 12.0% decrease in AU was noted overall. The VHA has also noted significantly declining AU against Gram-negative organisms resistant to multiple drugs, including carbapenems. Also, in a recent study from 2020 to 2021, the centrally coordinated network model of VHA long-term care units led to a decrease in days of antibiotic therapy by 21.7% (P=0.007) after case-based teaching on how to apply an evidence-based algorithm to distinguish urinary tract infection and asymptomatic bacteriuria. A retrospective analysis of DASON data from 2013 to 2018 showed that network-wide overall AU trends were flat during the first 12 months after network entry but decreased thereafter (relative rates, month 42 vs. month 13, 0.95 [95% CI, 0.91-0.99]). The centrally led network model of Atrium Health in the US showed that 78.6% (22/28) hospitals achieved their antibiotic reduction goals. In a retrospective study of a Centralized Health system Antimicrobial Stewardship Efforts program to expand antimicrobial stewardship to all University of Pittsburgh Medical Center hospitals regardless of local resources, AU at 13 hospitals decreased by 16% with a monthly change of -4.7 days of therapy/1,000 patient days (95% CI, -5.5 to -3.9; P <0.0001). In this study, the monthly change of AU of hospitals categorized into "non-robust" ASP hospitals, lacking core elements and dedicated resources, was not statistically different from that of "robust" hospitals meeting all core elements, including ID-trained pharmacists (P=0.16).

Proposed Korean ASP network models

Given the differences in the healthcare system and the availability of ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists between Korea and the US, applying the DASON network model to Korea may be challenging. It would be more appropriate to develop models tailored to Korea's circumstances and adopt a phased and gradual approach.

In the initial phase, loose collaborative relationships could be established. Activities such as sharing information and experiences related to ASP, conducting annual surveys to assess their current status, and organizing symposiums can serve as initial steps within the network. In the intermediate phase, efforts could focus on building a database system, implementing targeted actions to pick 'low-hanging fruit,' and providing educational materials and toolkits. Government funding is essential during the initial and intermediate phases to establish the ASP network model. In the advanced phase, expansion of network size, number of actions, and reinforcement of research could be tried. In this phase, business models that ensure the stainable and independent operation of ASP networks should be developed. Furthermore, policy support from the government would be critical to ensuring the successful implementation of these business models.

For the ASP network model in Korea, we proposed two types of approaches: the shared model and the hub-based model (Fig. 1). In the shared model, multiple hospitals with ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists form a network and share workloads and responsibilities to improve the quality and efficiency of ASP activities. For example, personnel with pharmacy/stewardship expertise in a network collectively work on tasks such as guideline and educational material development, database management, targeted implementation, and research for a network. A key advantage of the shared model is relative ease of establishment. However, it requires hospitals in the network to be relatively homogenous, and hospitals without experienced personnel to do shared workloads for the network may find it difficult to participate. Additionally, this model may fail if there is insufficient understanding and commitment to the concept and necessities of the ASP network. In the hub-based model, a hospital with experienced ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists for ASP provides services for ASP to hospitals with no or insufficient resources for ASP. This model enables the inclusion of hospitals without ID physicians or ID-trained pharmacists in ASP activities. However, it comes with the challenge of developing a business model to secure funding for the hub hospital's personnel and service provision.

Hurdles and Future Directions for securing pharmacy/stewardship expertise in Korea

The importance of securing more ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists as key perssonel as pharmacy/stewardship expertise in ASP can not be overestimated. Relatively low income and heavy workload make young doctors hesitant to become ID physicians in Korea. In a recent survey done in Korea, only 37.4% (73/352) of ID physicians and ID pediatricians responded that they were satisfied with their current job, and 37.0% of them felt that their work was inadequately compensated, particularly for infection control or ASP. Many pharmacists prefer working in private pharmacies over hospitals in Korea. The 2023 Department of Pharmacy Survey by the Korean Society of Health-System Pharmacists reported an 18% turnover rate among full-time hospital pharmacists, with 94.3% of those who left having less than five years of experience. This suggests that many new hospital pharmacists leave within five years, with a significant portion likely transitioning to positions in private pharmacies. In this situation, training a sufficient number of ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists is challenging. The Korean government should establish policies that ensure appropriate compensation for AS work and recognize expertise.

The government-led pilot project for ASP was launched in November 2024 in Korea. The National Health Insurance provides annual funding ranging from 320 million to 1.45 billion KRW for three years to hospitals that meet specific conditions, including ASP team formation, AS committee operations, development of local guidelines, audits, antimicrobial agent restrictions, participation in national AU surveillance, Clostridioides difficile infection monitoring, education, and reporting. Many non-ID-trained clinicians are expected to participate as ASP team members in this project. There is concern that these non-ID-trained clinicians may only be listed as ASP team members without engaging in meaningful AS activities. As the short-term strategies to address this issue, practical and applicable, target-oriented training and education should be provided to enable them to contribute effectively to ASP. Recognizing this need, education programs for ASP are currently being developed under government leadership. Additionally, adopting training and education programs from other countries to fit the Korean context can be a shortcut to increasing pharmacy/stewardship expertise. If well-structured education and training programs are established, issuing certification to non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists, qualifying them for ASP roles, could also be considered.

In Korea, where there is a shortage of pharmacy/stewardship expertise and relatively less experience with ASP, a network-based model led by ID physicians and/or ID-trained pharmacists could be an effective strategy for the nationwide expansion of ASP. It could be a win-win solution, recognizing the expertise of ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists while enhancing the performance of non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists for ASP. However, a lack of motivation of community hospitals to participate in such a network lead to limited adoption of the network-based support model in Korea. For long-term strategies, developing business models supported by government policy is essential to address this issue. For example, hospitals can get accreditation and additional points for better categorization in the previously mentioned pilot project by participating in an ASP network. In DASON, each hospital pays for the services, and they continue to participate because they consider it sufficiently cost-effective.
clinicians

In conclusion, although ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists are the priority personnel for accountability and pharmacy/stewardship expertise for ASP, non-ID-trained physicians and pharmacists can play an effective role in the nationwide expansion of ASP in Korea. A network-based model led by ID physicians and ID-trained pharmacists can be a good strategy to support these non-ID-trained  physicians and pharmacists. Securing pharmacy/stewardship expertise in Korea requires effort from the government to introduce supportive policies.

passages.text: Effects of BCAA supplementation on plasma and mare's milk amino acid contents in Yili mares and growth performance of suckling foals

Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) play a crucial role in regulating nutritional metabolism in lactating animals. However, limited research has been conducted on BCAAs in equines. This study aimed to investigate the effects of different doses of BCAA supplementation on plasma and milk amino acid profiles in Yili mares, as well as the growth performance of their suckling foals, thereby providing a scientific basis for optimizing feeding management practices. Eighteen pairs of Yili mares and their sucklings were randomly assigned to four groups: a control group (Group D, no BCAA supplementation) and three experimental groups (S1, S2, and S3, receiving 38 g/day, 76 g/day, and 114 g/day of BCAA supplementation, respectively). The trial lasted for 67 days. The concentrations of 22 amino acids in plasma and milk were quantified using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), and their correlations with the body height, length, and weight of the foals were analyzed using SPSS software (one-way analysis of variance and Pearson correlation test). In mare plasma amino acids, the serine (Ser) content in group S1 was significantly higher than that in group D (p < 0.05). Additionally, in group S3, tryptophan (Trp), histidine (His), and aspartic acid (Asp) contents were markedly elevated. For mare milk amino acids, Ser content in group S1 was extremely significantly higher than in group D (p < 0.01), while aspartic acid (Asp) and alanine (Ala) contents were significantly increased in group S3. Regarding foal growth performance, body weight in group S3 was significantly greater than in group D. Moreover, group S2 exhibited superior trends in body height and length growth. Correlation analysis demonstrated that plasma Ser and creatine (Cr) were positively correlated with mare milk Ser and Cr. Mare milk threonine (Thr) showed a positive correlation with foal body height and length. Studies indicate that branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) regulate protein synthesis and amino acid metabolism via the mTOR pathway. In this experiment, 38 g/d BCAA enhanced mammary gland Ser transport, thereby increasing its content. Furthermore, 114 g/d BCAA promoted Asp and Ala accumulation, likely due to enhanced catabolic activity. The positive correlation between mare milk Thr, His, and skeletal development suggests that BCAA indirectly promotes growth through milk composition regulation. However, given the small sample size of this study, long-term validation is necessary.
1 Introduction

Amino acids, the fundamental building blocks of proteins, play indispensable roles in governing physiological processes critical to animal growth, development, and reproductive success. Recent advancements in maternal amino acid supplementation strategies have expanded research frontiers in lactation modulation and offspring vitality enhancement. Lactating mares face exceptional metabolic demands to sustain both physiological homeostasis and milk synthesis, with nutritional status directly determining mare's milk compositional quality. Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA):leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), and valine (Val):constitute a distinctive category of essential amino acids that have attracted significant research attention for their regulatory functions in animal nutrient metabolism. Emerging evidence underscores BCAA's lactogenic potential in livestock production systems. Hultquist and Casper demonstrated that Val supplementation enhances milk yield in late-lactation dairy cattle. At the cellular level, Gao et al. revealed elevated Ile concentrations in bovine mammary epithelial cells stimulate sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1) expression, thereby promoting lipogenesis. Complementary findings by Wang identified a positive correlation between graded Leu supplementation in periparturient sow diets and progressive increases in milk lipid content. Most of the existing studies on BCAA in livestock production focus on animals such as cattle and pigs, and there are few studies on the specific effects of BCAA on the performance of equine animals. Especially in the feeding and management of mares during lactation, the effects of supplemental feeding of BCAA on the content of amino acids in plasma and milk of mares are still unclear. While existing studies have focused on the direct association between the high efficiency of mammary BCAA metabolism and milk component synthesis in ruminants, research on BCAA metabolism in horses is seriously lagging behind. This study systematically evaluates dose-dependent responses of plasma and mare's milk amino acid profiles to dietary BCAA supplementation, while establishing correlation matrices to decipher mammary amino acid utilization patterns (Figure 1). These findings are anticipated to provide theoretical foundations for optimizing feeding strategies and enhancing mare's milk quality in this economically vital equine population.

2 Materials and methods
2.1 Materials

The experiment utilized branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) obtained from Xinjiang Lianying Biotechnology Co., LTD. Following the amino acid requirement study for equine animals, the ratio of Isoleucine (Ile), Leucine (Leu), and Valine (Val) fed in the experiment was 1:2:1.2. The resulting mixture appeared as a white powder after thorough blending.
2.2 Design of experiments

The trial was conducted at Zhaosu Stud Farm in Yili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, from July to September 2023. Eighteen lactating mares (body weight: 392.90 kg +- 12.18 kg) and their suckling foals were randomly divided into four groups: a control group (Group D, n = 4) and three treatment groups (S1, S2, S3; n = 5, 5, 4, respectively). All mares were managed under identical feeding conditions for 67 d (7-d adaptation period and 60-d experimental phase). Each mare received 2 kg/d of concentrate supplement (composition and nutritional levels detailed in Table 1). Groups S1, S2, and S3 were additionally supplemented with 38, 76, and 114 g/d branched-chain amino acid (BCAA), respectively.

2.3 Feeding management

During the trial, mares and foals were moved daily at 10:00 h from pasture to the milking parlor. Following foal separation, mares were guided to individual stalls and supplemented with branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) at respective doses mixed into 2 kg of concentrate. Milking was performed every 1.5 h (four times/d). After the final milking session, mares and foals were returned to pasture for unrestricted grazing.
2.4 Sample collection and determination
2.4.1 Blood samples were collected from mares

On the 60th day of the experiment, mares were fasted for 2 h before blood samples were collected using EDTA anticoagulant. Specifically, 10 mL of blood was drawn from the jugular vein to obtain plasma, which was subsequently centrifuged at 3,000 r/min for 15 min. The resulting supernatant was then transferred to frozen storage tubes, promptly frozen in liquid nitrogen for 15 min, and finally stored in a refrigerator at -80 C for the analysis of free amino acid content.
2.4.2 Mare milk sample collection

Milk samples were collected on day 60 of the experiment and manually milked every 1.5 h (at 11:00, 12:30, 14:00, and 15:30, respectively). Subsequently, 25 mL from each of the four milk samples were combined, with 5 mL aliquoted into frozen tubes for rapid freezing in liquid nitrogen for 15 min, followed by storage at -80 C in a refrigerator. The free amino acid content in the milk was assessed using the identical determination index employed for plasma free amino acids.
2.4.3 Determination of free amino acid content

The detection was carried out by Beijing Novogene Technology Co., Ltd. using high performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) for quantitative analysis. The measured indexes include: Glycine (Gly), Serine (Ser), Methionine (Met), Proline (Pro), Leucine (Leu), Creatine (Cr), Glutamic (Glu), Phenylalanine (Phe), Lysine (Lys), Arginine (Arg), Tryptophan (Trp), Tyrosine (Tyr), Histidine (His), Valine (Val), Ornithine (Orn), Alanine (Ala), Isoleucine (Ile), Aspartic (Asp), Threonine (Thr), Taurine (Tau), glutamine (gln), asparaginate (asn).
2.4.4 Measurement of growth performance in suckling foals
Foals were restrained for measurement at 0 d and 60 d. Withers height, body length, chest girth, cannon bone circumference, and body weight were measured using a measuring stick and tape.
2.5 Data processing

Data were initially organized in Excel and analyzed using SPSS 26.0. One-way ANOVA with Duncan's multiple-range test was applied, with significance thresholds set at p < 0.05 (significant) and p < 0.01 (highly significant). Results are expressed as mean +- SD. To investigate correlations between plasma and mare's milk free amino acid content in Yili mares, as well as associations between milk amino acids and foal growth performance, Pearson correlation analysis was conducted in SPSS 21.0 using data from day 60. Figures were generated using Excel and the MetWare Cloud platform.
3 Results
3.1 Effects of BCAA supplementation on plasma free amino acid content of Yili mares

Figure 2 demonstrates that histogram of the quantitative results of plasma amino acid metabolome in mares. The plasma Asp concentrations in group S3 significantly exceeded those in D (p < 0.05, Figure 2B). Both S2 and S3 demonstrated higher His content than D (p < 0.05, Figure 2C), with S2 additionally surpassing S1 in His concentrations (p < 0.05). The Trp content in group S3 was significantly higher compared to that in group D (p < 0.05, Figure 2D), while showing comparable values to S1 and S2 (p > 0.05). Notably, Ser levels in groups D, S2, and S3 were significantly lower than those in S1 (p < 0.05, Figure 2E), with no significant differences detected among D, S2, and S3 (p > 0.05, Table 2).

3.2 Effect of BCAA supplementation on free amino acid content in Yili mare's milk

Figure 3 demonstrates that histogram of the quantitative results of the amino acid metabolome of Yili mare's milk. Figure 3B illustrates that group S3 exhibited elevated Ala concentrations compared to both D and S1 (p < 0.05), while demonstrating a more pronounced increase relative to S2 (p < 0.01) in mare's milk. The Ser concentrations in groups D, S2, and S3 were significantly lower than those in S1 (p < 0.05, Figure 3C), with no significant differences observed among D, S2, and S3 (p > 0.05, Table 3). Notably, Ser levels in S1 were substantially higher than in D (p < 0.01, Figure 3C). Similarly, Asp levels in S3 surpassed those in D and S2 (p < 0.05), with a highly significant difference compared to S1 (p < 0.01, Figure 3D).
